articles.title: Liberal-city resident hesitates when pressed on beliefs: 'I hadn't really thought about socialism that way'
articles.summary: Fox News Digital hit the streets of Portland, Maine, where residents offered sharply divided views on socialism, wealth inequality and capitalism.
articles.body:
PORTLAND, Maine — Americans who were asked for their opinions of socialism by Fox News Digital offered sharply different interpretations of the ideology, with some embracing its promises of economic equality while others expressed strong reservations about government control over the means of production.

Fox News Digital took to the streets of Maine's largest city , a progressive bastion, to talk to residents about their definitions of socialism and how far they would be willing to go to embrace its ideals.

The topic of socialism has featured prominently in campaign coverage during this midterm election cycle, as candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) scored high-profile victories over more centrist rivals in a slew of Democratic primaries this year. DSA's outsized influence has been a driving force in the ballot box battle for the Democratic Party's ideological future.

A new Fox News national poll indicates 32% of voters have a favorable view of socialism, with 64% seeing it in an unfavorable way. But the favorable rating matches an all-time high, first reached five years ago, since Fox News first began asking the question in 2019. And a September Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans had a positive image of socialism, the highest level since the polling organization began tracking the question in 2010.

Lewis, a retired Navy veteran, said socialism was a good thing because it "looks out for people's needs.... and it's not communism."

Socialism and communism both emphasize collective ownership of the means of production, such as factories, businesses and major industries. But socialism encompasses a range of approaches, including those that allow private enterprise, while communism traditionally envisions the abolition of private ownership of productive assets and, ultimately, a classless society.

Lewis turned skeptical when Fox News Digital asked whether he would personally surrender private property to government or collective control.

"I guess. I hadn't really thought about socialism that way. I think about taking care of the needs of people, you know, things like... national health care, things like that," he answered. "I don't like government taking things away from you."

Nolan, who recently moved to Portland, told Fox News Digital "there's a lot of wealth imbalance in America right now, and we could benefit from some sort of leveling system."

He said socialism exists to help "people who aren't as, you know, benefiting in society."

Nolan added that "business owners should have their autonomy" and that "people deserve to earn their money."

"But there are a lot of really high-end... corporations that benefit so much... that really don't need that much wealth... there's so much exorbitant wealth at the top end that a lot of that could trickle down to people who are disadvantaged and don't have homes," Nolan stated.

Nola, another resident passing through Portland's Monument Square, said socialism's "a good thing. It means equity."

Asked about the takeover of businesses and means of production under socialism, Nola said she still "100%" supported socialism.

"I'm the daughter of a small business owner. I've seen how tough it is to run a small business in this country and how easy it is for corporations to just do whatever they want," she explained. "So if we gave actually back to small businesses and the government helped them out... and so much of the market that's privatized actually became public, I think... with how big the U.S. has gotten, it's only a good thing."

"Socialism overall, I think it's a horrible idea," he emphasized. "If we can learn from history, anything from history, we see that it's gonna really give way too much power to the government institution. It's gonna... make things that are harmful overall for everyone... it's like it's dictatorship."

Ted argued that "socialism just impoverishes. Capitalism, the free market economy is a good thing."

He added that while "some people are very wealthy and very greedy," that overall capitalism "creates other wealth for other people."

The new Fox News poll found that 51% of voters had a favorable view of capitalism, compared with 32% who viewed socialism favorably. Another 46% had an unfavorable view of capitalism.

articles.title: Eleições no AM: Omar Aziz fala sobre atrair investimentos à Zona Franca de Manaus e Professora Maria do Carmo promete incentivos fiscais | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidatos ao governo do Amazonas cumpriram agendas de campanha nesta segunda-feira (19), em Manaus.
articles.summary: Candidatos ao governo do Amazonas cumpriram agendas de campanha nesta segunda-feira (19), em Manaus.
articles.body:
Omar Aziz (PSD) e Professora Maria do Carmo (PL) durante agenda em Manaus, nesta segunda-feira (19). — Foto: Rede Amazônica

Os candidatos ao governo do Amazonas, Omar Aziz (PSD) e Professora Maria do Carmo (PL), cumpriram agendas de campanha nesta segunda-feira (19), em Manaus , na disputa pelo segundo turno das eleições estaduais.

O candidato Omar Aziz participou de entrevista em uma rádio na capital amazonense e falou sobre incentivos fiscais, enquanto a candidata Professora Maria do Carmo participou de uma caminhada com apoiadores na Zona Centro-Sul da capital.

Omar Aziz terminou o primeiro turno na liderança para o cargo de governador do Amazonas, com 40,63% dos votos válidos (841.846 votos). Professora Maria do Carmo obteve 24,49% (507.335 votos). A votação do segundo turno está marcada para o dia 25 de outubro.

O candidato Omar Aziz participou, na manhã desta segunda, de uma entrevista à uma rádio em Manaus. Ainda durante a agenda, o candidato falou sobre incentivos fiscais para fomentar o empreendedorismo no estado. Ele também citou como a reforma tributária impacta a Zona Franca de Manaus e os desafios que o modelo enfrentará com essa mudança que passa a valer a partir de janeiro do próximo ano.

"Com a reforma tributária, o único local que você pode dar incentivo é a Zona Franca de Manaus. Os outros estados estão proibidos. Com isso, a competitividade nossa aumenta bastante e atrai novas indústrias. Eu tenho certeza que com nossa experiência, com o conhecimento que a gente tem, a gente vai não só manter essa competitividade em alta nível, mas também atrair novos segmentos."

Omar exerce atualmente o segundo mandato como senador pelo estado. Durante a campanha do segundo turno, tem defendido propostas voltadas ao desenvolvimento econômico e social, além de melhorias na saúde e na infraestrutura do Amazonas.

A candidata Professora Maria do Carmo, pela manhã, participou de uma caminhada por algumas ruas do bairro Parque Dez de Novembro, na Zona Centro-Sul da capital. Na rua do Comércio, foi recebida por lojistas e trabalhadores da região. Com o início das novas regras da reforma tributária, a candidata disse que é preciso se preparar para uma possível queda de arrecadação e que, em seu governo, vai criar incentivo fiscal e subsídio para o setor primário.

"A gente realmente vai ter que trabalhar fortemente com os incentivos como uma forma de alavancar nossa economia aqui, principalmente para as novas matrizes que a gente quer trazer. Isso é uma forma de você, é como se fosse um adiantamento pra que, depois, com a economia aquecida, ela consiga devolver pro governo aquilo que a gente usar pra incentivar", disse.

Professora Maria do Carmo disputa o cargo pela coligação "Mudar é Urgente", formada pelo Partido Liberal (PL). Em 2024, foi candidata a vice-prefeita de Manaus na chapa de Capitão Alberto Neto (PL). Em 2022, concorreu ao cargo de suplente do então candidato Arthur Neto (PSDB).

articles.title: The 2026 midterms are 2 weeks away. Which party has a better chance of winning? Here's what the latest polls say.
articles.summary: Trump's approval rating is going down. Democrats' lead on the generic ballot is going up. Could this be a "wave" election?
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm elections are just two weeks away. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data.

The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. Big events can, and often do, change the course of elections.

Yet the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too.

The state-by-state midterm landscape is finally taking shape — and a few clear polling trends are emerging. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears.

Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds).

You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading.

At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.4 percentage points) on the generic ballot. Two weeks later, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House .

At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.7 points on the generic ballot. Two weeks later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House .

Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But two weeks out, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a final Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House ; in 2010, those numbers were 9.4 points and 63 seats, respectively .

So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — about 9 percentage points , on average — and it has been steadily growing over the last month.

Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House.

National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow:

What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 4 percentage points . One recent poll shows a tie.

Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7 percentage points — over the last month.

What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . But some September polls showed a tie, or Sullivan slightly ahead.

Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrcian and former U.S. House candidate)

What the latest polls say : Graham holds a narrow lead in recent surveys . But it is small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well.

Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong.

Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability

To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle.

At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them.

According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 60% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 38% who approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at 22%.

Again, history can provide perspective . In mid-September 2018, Trump was about 12 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November.

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 73% disapprove and 24% approve. That's a 49-point gap.

In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection.

articles.title: Ro Khanna sparks backlash over France riot comments as critic says he wants to ‘ride the rage wave’
articles.summary: Ro Khanna argued France riots show a need to "listen to our young," drawing sharp backlash from critics who accused him of excusing political violence.
articles.body:
Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., a potential 2028 presidential contender, drew criticism from across the political spectrum after pointing to the riots in France as a warning about wealth inequality and urging the U.S. to "listen to our young."

"This is what happens when the nations let wealth and power accumulate in the hands of a few," Khanna wrote in a post to X on Sunday evening.

Khanna's post comes on the heels of nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living and public services that descended into violence, looting and arson in several French cities on Saturday, prompting critics to accuse the progressive Democrat of giving political legitimacy to the destruction.

Spencer Pratt , former mayoral candidate for Los Angeles, blasted what he saw as an attempt to side with rioters.

"Of course Rohit Conman sees mass communist riots destroying businesses and historic buildings in Paris and lies about it as some noble 'ask' for justice," Pratt wrote.

"These commies lie as easily as they breathe."

The comment also drew criticism from Shannon Watts, a Democratic gun activist who, in recent months, has criticized the far-left portions of her party.

"If you're a member of Congress who condemned the January 6 insurrection, you don't get to excuse riots in France as a 'cry for help.' Political violence doesn't become acceptable just because you sympathize with people committing it," Watts wrote in a post of her own.

Still others warned Khanna against using the moment as a way to build political momentum.

"Ro Khanna has long sought to ride the rage wave to power," Jonathan Turley, a political commentator and legal analyst, said.

"Khanna could indeed learn much from France. This is history repeating itself. That history, by the way, does not bode well for establishment figures who pander to the mob," Turley added, giving a nod to the infamous French Revolution that targeted the country's political and financial elite in a bloody crusade.

Planned demonstrations in France over the weekend quickly spiraled out of control on Saturday, leaving behind broken storefronts and fires in Paris.

French authorities said that by Sunday evening they had arrested nearly 2,400 people nationwide, including 855 in the Paris region. Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, seven seriously, according to France's Interior Ministry. One protester died after suffering cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris, authorities said.

In Limoges, a fire that authorities said was deliberately set at the city hall caused significant damage to the historic building. Shops were looted in Paris, Bordeaux, Marseille, Lyon and other cities, while public buildings were vandalized or targeted by fires.

Authorities estimated that more than 550,000 people participated in demonstrations across France. Organizers put the figure at roughly 800,000.

Despite the mayhem, Khanna argued the moment should prompt American lawmakers to take younger voters' political demands more seriously, especially on topics of equity.

"This is what happens when young people lose hope in their future. In America, let us listen to our young. We need an economic and political transformation. America's Next New Deal," Khanna wrote.

"From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: in an age of massive wealth inequality, they want a future they can believe in," Khanna wrote.

But in the face of the backlash online, Khanna quickly clarified his stance in a follow-up post, noting that he did not support the destruction that had unfolded.

"I unequivocally condemn violence and vandalism. I have always championed my grandfather's example of non-violent protest," Khanna wrote, referencing his relative, Amarnath Vidyalankar, who was imprisoned for advocating for India's independence in the early 1930s.

"Let us not be blind to the anger young people have against the unholy alliance of wealth and power. The billionaires buying politicians. The corruption," Khanna added.

But even after issuing his clarifying statement, Khanna continued to face condemnation — even from figures like former Rep. George Santos, R-N.Y.

"These are not mere students… my friend, I regret to inform you, this is an invasion," Santos wrote, referring to France's high intake of refugees in recent years.

Khanna, responding to Santos, doubled down on his view.

"George, is the lesson not to tackle the vast disparity here and young people's hopelessness?" he asked.

Khanna's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital.

Bradford Benz contributed to this report

articles.title: Trump approval rating falls to career low in new poll
articles.summary: The president’s sinking numbers come as early voting began in several states, with the GOP facing an uphill battle to maintain control of Congress.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen to a new record low, with less than one-third of Americans approving of the president's job performance, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll .

The poll, released on Oct. 19, found Trump's approval rating at 31%, the lowest the president has seen in Reuters/Ipsos tracking in either term, and a one-point dip from his previous career low recorded two weeks ago.

The president's sinking approval rating comes as early voting began in several states, with Republicans facing an uphill battle to maintain slim majorities in Congress.

Democrats are currently ahead of the GOP by 12 percentage points in a new generic congressional ballot, the widest lead the party has held in Reuters/Ipsos tracking this election cycle.

The four-day Reuters/Ipsos poll surveyed 1,679 U.S. adults and has a 2-percentage-point margin of error.

Terrible, horrible, no good, very bad polls

Trump's bad poll follows two other scathing surveys released on Oct. 18.

In a new Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll , Trump's approval rating hit a record low for the pollster, reaching 33%. That was a 4-point dip from a July poll and an 8-point drop from one in October 2025.

The same poll found Democrats, for the first time in a decade, were more trusted to deal with the economy than Republicans.

Donald Trump's second term: Actions, travels of the 47th president

In an NBC News/SurveyMonkey poll released the same day, Trump's approval rating fell to a second-term low of 34%, with 51% of respondents "strongly disapproving" of the president's job performance. Among Latino voters, who shifted toward Trump in 2024, the president's approval rating sat at 31%.

In another second-term record for the president, 71% said the country was on the "wrong track," up 10 percentage points from another poll in April 2025.

The same poll also found Democrats were 10 percentage points ahead of the GOP in a generic congressional ballot.

Polling averages show a continuous slide

Including the three bad polls for the president in the last two days, broader polling averages also show Trump sliding into deeper negative territory.

As of Monday, Oct. 19, the RealClearPolitics average showed Trump with a 38.9% approval rating and a 59.3% disapproval rating. The New York Times polling average had Trump at 37% approval and 61% disapproval, while Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin average showed 37.5% approval and 59.9% disapproval.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

articles.title: GOP lawmakers scramble to spare Ukraine from Trump
articles.summary: Lawmakers are struggling to find a way to convince the president to stop cozying up to Russia.
articles.body:
Republican lawmakers are incensed about President Donald Trump's dismissal of Ukraine — and powerless to stop him.

That frustration hit a new peak on Monday as they sought to address the president's decision to purchase Russian diesel, waive sanctions on Moscow and potentially stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Those moves, coupled with days of unexplained disruptions in Kyiv's U.S.-controlled satellite defenses, left them freelancing remedies to address the new rift between Washington and Kyiv.

Senate Armed Services Committee members urged Trump to strike a deal with Ukraine that would curb its strikes on Russian energy targets. Another group of lawmakers held an emergency call with Ukraine's leader. A third faction threatened to derail the administration's lame-duck agenda.

The disparate responses reflect an undercurrent of Republican angst about an administration that has largely ignored Congress on Ukraine and foreign policy more broadly — and the lack of a coordinated response from the legislative branch. And they underscore just how little power Trump's own party has had in reining in his attacks on longstanding allied relationships.

"Democrats and Republicans in Congress understand what will happen if [President Vladimir] Putin faces no consequences for his murderous invasion," Sens. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said after a last-minute call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meant to assure him the U.S. is still a partner.

Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions was particularly painful for lawmakers, who passed a bill to impose them in September after more than a year of congressional maneuvering and resistance from the White House. That legislation also granted Trump the power to waive sanctions, which he did almost immediately.

Now both Republicans and Democrats are scrambling to determine what the next steps should entail if Trump doesn't change course. But they acknowledge they're running low on options.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) told reporters on Monday that "it's going to be difficult to say anything in the next two weeks that's going to make any difference" on Ukraine.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) publicly pleaded with Trump to support a plan in which Ukraine would halt strikes on Russian oil refineries in exchange for information from the U.S. on the Kremlin's missile and drone launch sites.

"President Trump can lower prices at the pump today by simply agreeing to this deal!" Wicker said in a social media post . "MR. PRESIDENT, PLEASE TAKE THIS WIN!"

The White House, when asked for comment, referred to Trump's recent remarks to reporters that he supported stopping the war. "Why? Because that's what I do for a living," he said. "And frankly, Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it, but I want to see people not die."

Trump has said his moves are intended to facilitate a peace deal between Kyiv and Moscow, after a grueling war that has dragged on for more than four years. But his actions have troubled even some of the president's most stalwart defenders.

Rep. Craig Goldman (R-Texas), who won Trump's endorsement for re-election this year, told reporters he was in favor of keeping sanctions on Russia in place.

Another Trump-aligned lawmaker, Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), said he agreed ending the war was in the U.S. national interest. But, he added, the administration should pressure Russia to stop fighting, "rather than buy their oil and hold our Ukrainian allies back from using their full combat potential."

Others threatened to derail the Trump administration's lame duck priorities, most notably blocking the president's proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget, which hinges on unified GOP support in the face of staunch Democratic opposition.

"The agenda is dead," said retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), a frequent Trump critic. "Many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus."

And Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Penn.) pledged that anyone who attempted to limit the use of Starshield — a Pentagon-controlled satellite network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX — for Ukraine would be "fully investigated and held accountable" via oversight hearings and harsh budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head.

Any oversight action could still take months to materialize. And Trump has successfully maneuvered around Congress in the past, such as leaving top officials in acting roles because they won't receive enough Senate backing to get confirmed.

Democrats insisted they were working with Republicans to counter Trump's embrace of Russia, although they didn't detail exactly what those responses would be.

Blumenthal, in a follow-up post on social media, said lawmakers would express their support for Ukraine in "upcoming action" but did not specify what that meant.

In the interim, Trump's actions toward Russia and Ukraine have mystified lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Rep. Madeline Dean (D-Pa.), who sits on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in an MS NOW interview after the Zelenskyy call, that lawmakers asked if he understood why the White House was undermining Ukraine's war footing. He could not provide any explanation.

"I find it historically dishonorable that the president has turned and showed his cards," she said, "that he supports Mr. Putin in this effort, the one who is bloodthirsty and has cost tens of thousands of lives."

Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy contributed to this report.

articles.title: GOP attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith come to a head in heated town hall exchange
articles.summary: The Muslim Brotherhood has become a flashpoint in Michigan’s Senate race, with Republicans trying to connect Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to the group.
articles.body:
The Muslim Brotherhood has become a flashpoint in Michigan's Senate race, with Republicans trying to cast Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terror and El-Sayed arguing that he is being unfairly accused of the same "dual loyalties" that former Presidents John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama once were.

El-Sayed this weekend denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement founded in Egypt in 1928 — first in a heated exchange with a voter, and later when speaking with reporters — after Republicans have sought to highlight his family's ties to the group and his past comments about it.

"I do want to talk about why they want to make this their closing argument," El-Sayed told reporters after a rally Sunday in Flint. "They want to speak to a certain implicit dual loyalty. This has a long history in our politics, that notion that people might pray a little bit differently, have a dual loyalty. It was the same thing they did to JFK when he ran for president, the notion that because he was Catholic that he somehow had dual loyalties. They did the same thing to President Obama simply because his father was of Muslim origin, even though his father is an avowed Christian."

He added: "This is nothing new. This is what they do when they have no message about the real issues in people's lives."

Republicans have increasingly drawn attention to El-Sayed's Muslim faith in the closing weeks of one of the most important Senate races on the 2026 midterm election map.

President Donald Trump, at a campaign rally Friday night, referred to El-Sayed as "Mohammed" and falsely declared that the Democratic former public health official is a "jihadist." Those comments have become staples of recent Trump rallies and social media comments.

El-Sayed's Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, said Sunday on CNN that he has "never called him a terrorist" and said he does not "speak for the president."

But Rogers accused El-Sayed of aligning with the Muslim Brotherhood.

The Muslim Brotherhood is an Islamist movement with global offshoots that once wielded significant political power in Egypt, where it was founded. The movement officially rejects the use of violent means to secure its goals. However, offshoots of the group have been linked to attacks in the past.

Trump signed an executive order in November that initiated a process by which certain chapters or other subdivisions of the Muslim Brotherhood could be considered for designation as Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

"You know, he wants to play the victim. This is not about that. This is about the way you think, not the way you pray," Rogers told CNN's Dana Bash. "This is about your ideology and how dangerous it is."

The GOP efforts to tie El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, and Islamic extremism, burst into the open this weekend at a town hall in Caro.

An attendee repeatedly pressed El-Sayed about the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he had yet to hear the candidate reject the organization.

"Abdul, will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?" the man shouted from the crowd.

El-Sayed, after disavowing the movement, blasted the man for implicitly assuming his "dual loyalty."

"You assume … that because I am Muslim, that somehow I would have some allegiance to something that is not our Constitution," El-Sayed said. He later added, "For me, that Constitution is the guiding light."

The audience member walked out after the exchange as the crowd cheered for El-Sayed.

The GOP attacks come after old tweets from El-Sayed's half-sister resurfaced online, including a post from 2012 in which she described having "an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college."

El-Sayed has said he does not know what his mother was doing in Egypt during the 1970s, explaining he was 3 when his parents divorced and didn't see his mother for years. He was primarily raised in Michigan by his father and stepmother.

El-Sayed in 2012 also signed an open letter supporting then-Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who had been elected earlier that year with the support of the Muslim Brotherhood after the overthrow of the country's authoritarian government.

A year earlier, he penned a Huffington Post op-ed calling on the United States to support young Arab protesters in Egypt, and downplaying concerns that supporting democracy there would lead to Muslim Brotherhood control of the nation.

During a recent debate, Rogers pointed out that El-Sayed's mother worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, a non-profit that the Treasury Department in 2004 designated as an organization supporting terrorism.

"Are you going after my mom?" said El-Sayed.

"I was going after that organization that was indicted for funneling money to Al Qaeda," Rogers said. "Look, that's your mom. My mom worked at a small chamber of commerce. I'll put my mom up any day for that."

El-Sayed responded he is a "dad and a doctor" who wants to "get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for All." He said Rogers "wants this to be about anything but his own record."

El-Sayed in recent days also addressed his sister-in-law, Mariam Jukaku, being placed on the federal Terrorism Screening Database — a situation she challenged as part of a 2016 class action lawsuit . It's not clear why Jukaku, who was once p resident of UCLA's Muslim Student Association and is now a home-school teacher and writer in California , was added to the list.

"She did nothing wrong and was captured on that and then sued and got off," El-Sayed told Fox News when asked about his wife's sister being placed on the terrorist watchlist, which was created in the wake of the September 11, 2001, attacks. "You've got this system where folks are guilty until proven innocent because they've got different kinds of names, because of the infrastructure that people like Mike Rogers set up."

CNN's Jeff Zeleny and Aleena Fayaz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democratic senator sparks controversy over comments on investigating the Trump administration
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin is drawing criticism from President Donald Trump and other prominent Republicans after suggesting congressional investigations...
articles.body:
Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin is drawing criticism from President Donald Trump and other prominent Republicans after suggesting congressional investigations could deter recent graduates from joining the Trump administration.

The controversy stemmed from Slotkin's remarks at a University of Chicago event last week, when she was asked how Congress could reassert its role as a check on the Trump administration. Slotkin said if Democrats regained the majority in Congress, they should look to pass major domestic bills and use their oversight powers to focus on "signature" examples of corruption by the Trump administration, targeting not just the president, but also aides who did his "bidding."

"I wanna look at these signature cases and not just focus on the president but on the people who enabled him," the Michigan Democrat said. "I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration?' … I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want. And so let me avoid participating in that.' I want that deterrence message sent."

The remarks sparked backlash from Republicans, including Trump, who on Monday called Slotkin a "lowlife who's ruining her state."

"What they're doing is really discouraging people from going into politics. No, a weaponized government of Democrats, that's what they've done," Trump said when asked about the senator's remarks.

Sen. Mike Lee accused Slotkin of threatening young, politically inclined Americans. Mike Davis, the head of a conservative legal group, accused her of trying to scare young people away from government and wrote she should "learn about the Second ​Amendment, sweetheart."

Slotkin said Davis, in those comments, was suggesting she be shot, and that it amounted to the mobilization of "death threats" against her and her staff "for sport."

Davis later said, "Elissa Slotkin can pretend she's the victim all she wants, but she expressly called for the arrest of political opponents to deter their young supporters from public service. That is textbook fascism."

The controversy over the comments comes in the final sprint to the midterm elections with Democrats increasingly optimistic they could win the House and potentially even the Senate. Both parties are already bracing for what is expected to be an outpouring of congressional investigations into the Trump administration if Democrats prevail.

A group that identifies itself as the University of Chicago's "leading student-run conservative & libertarian publication" clipped a portion of Slotkin's comments in an X post, which has been viewed over 7 million times. In response to that clip, Lee wrote, "It is absolutely disgraceful to threaten young Americans for participating in politics and serving their country."

Slotkin said in response on X that the Utah Republican was "lying about what I said," and wrote, "spare us the manufactured outrage."

The Michigan senator noted in her post and in an interview with CNN that she was the target of Trump's Justice Department, which investigated her and other Democratic lawmakers after they posted a video urging service members and intelligence officials to disobey any illegal orders from the administration.

"My point is, do not get yourself involved in illegal activity," she said Monday evening on "The Lead." "It's the same thing I was talking about a year ago. Whether you're the uniformed military or a civilian in government, if you're being asked to do something by the president or his team that's illegal, you have a responsibility to reject that. That is my point."

Other Trump administration officials, including Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor, have chastised Slotkin's comments.

"This is incredibly disappointing and unprofessional coming from a US Senator - endorsing political prosecutions to dissuade patriotic Americans from serving their country," he wrote. "In contrast, we at @USOPM believe in recruiting the best and brightest early career prospects."

This story has been updated with additional developments.

articles.title: Presos do Oeste Paulista trocam quase um milhão de cartas em 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Números disponibilizados pela Secretaria da Administração Penitenciária (SAP) ao g1 reforçam a reintegração entre os detentos e as famílias.
articles.summary: Presos e familiares de unidades prisionais da região de Presidente Prudente (SP) trocaram quase um milhão de cartas entre janeiro e setembro deste ano, conforme a SAP.
articles.body:
Complexo Penal de Tupi Paulista (SP) — Foto: Gustavo Luz/TV TEM

Presos e familiares de unidades prisionais da região de Presidente Prudente (SP) trocaram quase um milhão de cartas entre janeiro e setembro deste ano, conforme a Secretaria da Administração Penitenciária (SAP).

Os números disponibilizados pela SAP ao g1 reforçam a reintegração social entre os detentos e as famílias.

Nas unidades da Coordenadoria de Execução Penal da Região Oeste do estado (Ceproeste), que inclui 36 complexos penais e unidades prisionais, de janeiro a setembro deste ano, foram enviadas 539.818 correspondências e recebidas 431.769 .

Em 2025, também nas unidades da Ceproeste, foram 625.345 correspondências enviadas e 512.400 recebidas, enquanto, em 2024, foram 637.978 enviadas e 530.957 recebidas.

Considerando todas as unidades prisionais do estado de São Paulo, em 2025, foram enviadas mais de 1,6 milhão de correspondências e recebidas 1,6 milhão. Em 2024, foram 1,5 milhão de correspondências enviadas e quase 1,5 milhão recebidas.

Conforme a Polícia Penal do Estado de SP, as correspondências recebidas e expedidas pelas pessoas presas são recepcionadas pelos setores de Portaria e Segurança.

O chefe de Serviço Regional Oeste do Programa de Atenção à Pessoa Egressa e Família, Jean Zocatelli, explicou que a troca de cartas é um direito garantido por lei e também contribui para fortalecer os vínculos afetivos.

"A correspondência entre as pessoas privadas de liberdade e seus familiares, assegurada pela Lei de Execução Penal, constitui importante instrumento para a preservação e o fortalecimento dos vínculos familiares, contribuindo para a manutenção dos laços afetivos durante o período de privação de liberdade", destacou.

Presos e familiares de unidades prisionais do Oeste Paulista trocam quase 1 milhão de cartas em 2026 — Foto: Reprodução/SAP

Antes da entrega aos respectivos destinatários, as cartas passam por conferência da identificação do remetente e do destinatário, inspeção física e demais procedimentos de fiscalização previstos.

Segundo a Secretaria da Administração Penitenciária, em casos de indícios de irregularidade nas cartas, são adotadas as providências administrativas cabíveis.

Esta atividade integra a rotina operacional dos estabelecimentos penais e é executada por policiais penais designados conforme a necessidade do serviço, segundo a pasta.

A SAP também informou que não há um quantitativo fixo de servidores exclusivamente destinado a essa atribuição.

Além disso, também não é possível contabilizar individualmente as correspondências recebidas e enviadas por cada reeducanda. No caso, é feito um quantitativo geral das correspondências movimentadas.

Dentre as detentas que costumam trocar cartas com a família, está a advogada e influenciadora Deolane Bezerra, presa em Tupi Paulista (SP). Em uma das correspondências, enviada à mãe dela, Solange Bezerra, e divulgada nas redes sociais no dia 8 de setembro , a influenciadora afirma que está bem e que foi vítima de uma “acusação falsa”.

Solange Bezerra compartilhou a carta da filha, Deolane, nas redes sociais; advogada está presa por suposto envolvimento com o PCC — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Se as cartas garantem o vínculo por escrito, por telefone a comunicação com as unidades costuma enfrentar dificuldades. No início de outubro, diversas famílias entraram em contato com o g1 após não conseguirem contato com a Penitenciária Feminina de Tupi Paulista (SP).

A unidade conta com ao menos 12 números diferentes de telefone com o código 018 de Discagem Direta à Distância (DDD), e eles não funcionavam.

Os motivos do contato da família com a unidade prisional são para confirmar vários assuntos, como a renovação da carteirinha para visitação, documentação e a situação da reeducada, segundo os relatos.

Em nota, a SAP afirmou que as linhas telefônicas da unidade apresentavam instabilidade em decorrência de falhas em equipamentos externos. Os reparos já estavam sendo realizados pelo setor técnico competente.

Segundo as famílias, a situação foi normalizada a partir de terça-feira, 13 de outubro , após ficarem sem conseguir contato desde o dia 4 de setembro. A SAP também confirmou que o sistema de telefonia foi restabelecido na data.

Além disso, a Polícia Penal do Estado de São Paulo informou que os canais de atendimento digital da Penitenciária Feminina de Tupi Paulista permanecem ativos e operantes.

A SAP orientou que os atendimentos aos familiares e ao público externo estavam sendo feitos por WhatsApp automatizado, no número (18) 3851-9628, e por e-mail: pftupi@sp.gov.br.

articles.title: Assédio eleitoral no trabalho: MPT registra 35 denúncias por dia | G1
articles.standfirst: Em setembro de 2026, o aumento nesse tipo de denúncia foi de 713% em relação ao mesmo mês de 2022, aponta levantamento do Ministério Público do Trabalho.
articles.summary: Assédio eleitoral no trabalho gera 35 denúncias diárias ao MPT, que utiliza inteligência artificial para identificar crimes e punir empresas irregulares em todo o país.
articles.body:
Assédio eleitoral no trabalho — Foto: Arte/GloboNews

O Brasil registrou uma média de 35 denúncias de assédio público eleitoral por dia, em outubro, de acordo com dados do Ministério Público do Trabalho. O levantamento foi feito até o dia 19, quando 663 denúncias já haviam sido registradas.

Assédio eleitoral no trabalho é quando o empregador tenta interferir na escolha do voto do empregado.

➡️Por exemplo, com ameaças de perda de emprego, rebaixamento de cargo ou de salário caso vote em determinado candidato. Ou ainda quando é feita entrega de santinhos ou quando são realizados eventos políticos dentro do ambiente do trabalho.

Em setembro deste ano, o MPT já havia registrado um aumento expressivo de 713% nas denúncias desse tipo em relação ao mesmo mês das eleições anteriores, de 2022. Enquanto naquele ano foram registradas 68 denúncias, em setembro de 2026 foram 553.

As principais vítimas, de acordo com a Pasta, são trabalhadores da iniciativa privada. Geralmente, pessoas de menor renda, que são mais vulneráveis ao poder econômico do empregador.

No caso dos servidores públicos, são afetados especialmente os que ocupam cargos comissionados e podem ser pressionados pelos gestores.

O crescimento de denúncias, no entanto, não reflete, necessariamente, um aumento de casos. Há cada vez mais uma conscientização da sociedade de que assédio eleitoral é crime, o que estimula as denúncias.

Algumas ações do MPT também ajudam a explicar a alta nos registros. Entre elas, plantões eleitorais que passaram a ser feitos nos finais de semana.

Também foram firmados acordos de cooperação técnica para troca mais rápida de informações entre a Pasta e outros órgãos, como o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral e o Ministério Público Eleitoral.

Outra novidade deste ano é o uso de inteligência artificial para classificar e organizar as denúncias de forma automática.

A tecnologia identifica, por exemplo, se denúncias diferentes foram feitas sobre uma mesma empresa e classifica qual o tipo de irregularidade cometida. Ou seja, é possível mapear a situação de maneira mais ágil.

As denúncias podem ser feitas de maneira anônima no site do Ministério Público do Trabalho. Uma vez feita a denúncia, o MPT investiga os fatos e entra em contato com a empresa.

Neste ano, 36 termos de ajustamento de conduta já foram firmados entre o MPT e empresas. Em caso de resistência, essas denúncias podem virar ações civis públicas. Até o momento, em 2026, 25 ações já foram ajuizadas. Destas, 24 tiveram liminares concedidas.

Em caso de descumprimento da liminar, a empresa paga multa e indenização por dano moral coletivo.

O procurador-geral do trabalho, Gláucio Araújo Oliveira, afirma que o assédio eleitoral no trabalho representa um risco à democracia.

"Se nós não frearmos essas condutas, ditadas pelo poder econômico ou pelo domínio na administração pública, isso representa um grave risco à nossa democracia porque é uma das formas de interferência na vontade popular que se manifesta na hora do voto, nas urnas."

articles.title: Jefferson da Linave: quem era o secretário de Queimados morto pela PM | G1
articles.standfirst: Casado e pai de uma filha, Jefferson entrou para a política em 2004, quando disputou pela 1ª vez uma vaga na Câmara Municipal de Queimados pelo Partido Trabalhista Brasileiro (PTB).
articles.summary: Jefferson da Linave era secretário de Queimados e empresário com longa trajetória política, morto em ação da PM na Avenida Brasil após suposta ordem de parada.
articles.body:
O secretário municipal de Desenvolvimento Econômico de Queimados e ex-vereador Jefferson Dias da Silva , o Jefferson da Linave , morreu após ser baleado na noite desta segunda-feira (19) na Avenida Brasil , na altura da estação do BRT Marinha Mercante, na Penha, Zona Norte do Rio de Janeiro.

Jefferson tinha 51 anos e era empresário do ramo de transporte e do mercado imobiliário. Casado e pai de uma filha, teve mais de 20 anos de vida pública. Disputou 5 eleições, sendo eleito em 3 delas.

Jefferson entrou para a política em 2004, quando disputou pela 1ª vez uma vaga na Câmara Municipal de Queimados pelo Partido Trabalhista Brasileiro (PTB). Naquele ano, foi eleito com pouco mais de 800 votos.

Em 2008, foi novamente eleito vereador. Dois anos depois, em 2010, concorreu ao cargo de deputado federal, mas não conseguiu se eleger.

Entre 2011 e 2019, Jefferson não ocupou cargos eletivos. Em 2020, voltou à Câmara Municipal ao ser novamente eleito vereador de Queimados. Já em 2024, não obteve votos suficientes para permanecer no Legislativo municipal e acabou nomeado pelo prefeito Glauco Kaizer secretário municipal de Desenvolvimento Econômico de Queimados.

Naquele ano, declarou quase R$ 1 milhão em bens à Justiça Eleitoral.

Jefferson Dias, conhecido como Jefferson da Linave, tinha 51 anos e exerceu 3 mandatos de vereador em Queimados — Foto: Reprodução

O g1 apurou que Jefferson estava voltando de um compromisso na Barra da Tijuca, na Zona Sudoeste do Rio, e estava sozinho em um BYD . Não se sabe para onde ele estava seguindo. O secretário tinha uma casa em Queimados.

Segundo testemunhas, Jefferson teria desobedecido a uma ordem de parada policial. Ainda de acordo com os relatos, policiais dispararam contra o automóvel. O secretário parou metros à frente.

Vídeos gravados por outros motoristas mostram ao menos 2 agentes efetuando disparos em direção ao veículo.

As circunstâncias da ocorrência ainda serão investigadas pela Delegacia de Homicídios da Capital (DHC), na Barra da Tijuca, onde os policiais envolvidos na ação prestaram depoimento.

O prefeito de Queimados, Glauco Kaizer, esteve no local e acompanhou a perícia da Polícia Civil . Nas redes sociais, o político lamentou a morte do secretário.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: acompanhe a apuração em todo o Brasil  | G1

articles.summary: Com atualização em tempo real, página do g1 vai acompanhar a apuração das urnas em todo o país. A home do portal também terá funcionalidades para facilitar o acompanhamento dos resultados.
articles.body:
Eleições 2026: apuração em tempo real — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Acompanhe a apuração das eleições 2026 ao vivo pelo g1 neste domingo (25). Além da disputa pela Presidência da República, cinco estados e o Distrito Federal terão segundo turno para a escolha de seus governadores.

Os dados abaixo são do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) .

Na página de apuração do g1 , o usuário pode acessar os números de votos em cada unidade federativa em tempo real e acompanhar a apuração.

Além das páginas de apuração, o g1 terá uma série de recursos especiais para facilitar o acompanhamento das Eleições 2026. Resultados em tempo real, vídeo ao vivo, mapas interativos e conteúdos automatizados estarão disponíveis nas homes e em páginas especiais do portal (veja abaixo).

Apuração das Eleições 2026: acompanhe os resultados em tempo real

Além da apuração nacional, acesse diretamente as páginas com os resultados do segundo turno nos cinco estados e no Distrito Federal:

O que você encontra na página de apuração

Ao acessar o estado desejado, você encontrará um resumo da corrida eleitoral da região, começando pela lista dos candidatos . Também é possível acessar o resumo da corrida presidencial.

Até as 17h de domingo (25), os candidatos estarão listados por ordem alfabética. Conforme os dados da apuração forem liberados pelo TSE, os nomes serão listados de acordo com a quantidade de votos recebidos.

Em seguida, um gráfico mostrará, do início ao fim da apuração, a evolução dos candidatos mais bem colocados ( imagem abaixo ).

Será possível navegar pelos mapas interativos do Brasil e dos estados para ver os resultados da eleição para presidente nos 5.571 municípios.

Em 108 cidades e no Distrito Federal, a consulta será ainda mais detalhada: além do resultado por zona eleitoral e local de votação, o eleitor poderá conferir os votos de sua própria urna.

Página de apuração tem link para mapa com números locais — Foto: Reprodução

Mapa de Minas Gerais na página de apuração — Foto: g1

Outras funcionalidades no g1 nas Eleições 2026

Além das páginas de apuração, o g1 terá novas funcionalidades nas Eleições 2026 para facilitar o acompanhamento dos resultados pelos eleitores.

Ao acessar o g1 , o leitor encontrará uma régua de apuração com os candidatos mais bem colocados e a atualização dos resultados em tempo real.

A funcionalidade estará disponível na home principal do g1 e nas páginas de Política e de Eleições das afiliadas do g1 em todo o Brasil, a partir das 7h do domingo (25).

As homes do g1, de Política e das afiliadas também terão um vídeo ao vivo com a cobertura nacional da TV e as principais informações sobre a apuração em todo o Brasil. A transmissão estará disponível a partir das 14h de domingo (25).

As homes do g1 , das afiliadas e suas páginas de Eleições também terão um mapa com a apuração em todo o Brasil. A experiência será a mesma disponível na home principal do g1 , com uma visão nacional dos resultados. O mapa ficará logo abaixo da manchete.

A cobertura especial das Eleições 2026 no g1 também terá uma página com mapas interativos, que permitirão aos eleitores navegar por todas as regiões do Brasil e acompanhar os resultados da votação em cada localidade.

Exemplo do mapa de apuração — Foto: Reprodução/g1

Textos automatizados e ferramentas exclusivas

A cobertura das Eleições 2026 no g1 também contará com uma série de conteúdos produzidos de forma automatizada, com ajuda de inteligência artificial e sob a supervisão de jornalistas.

Os textos vão permitir ao eleitor consultar candidatos e resultados da votação com diferentes níveis de detalhamento:

Quem são os candidatos : ferramenta com informações sobre os candidatos que disputam as eleições;

Cidades por estado : página que reúne os municípios de cada estado e permite acessar informações sobre as cidades e, em seguida, os locais de votação;

Resultados por cidade: página que reúne os municípios de cada estado para consulta dos resultados da votação;

Como foi a votação por cidade: conteúdo publicado assim que a votação for concluída no município;

Como foi a votação por local de votação: detalhamento dos votos por urna e por local de votação, disponível assim que a votação for concluída na cidade.

articles.title: Ponte Presidente Dutra e centro de Petrolina têm interdição hoje | G1
articles.standfirst: Para evitar transtornos, motoristas devem usar a Orla ou a Avenida das Nações como rotas alternativas.
articles.summary: A interdição na Ponte Presidente Dutra começa às 16h desta terça-feira (20); motoristas devem usar a Orla e a Avenida das Nações como rotas alternativas.
articles.body:
Trânsito na ponte Presidente Dutra no sentido Juazeiro — Foto: Reprodução /Ammpla

O centro de Petrolina , no Sertão de Pernambuco, terá mudanças no trânsito nesta terça-feira (20) por causa de um ato político. A principal alteração é a interdição total da Ponte Presidente Dutra, que liga a cidade a Juazeiro (BA), a partir das 16h.

Segundo a Autarquia Municipal de Mobilidade (AMMPLA), o Viaduto dos Barranqueiros e um trecho da Avenida Guararapes também serão bloqueados. A interdição na avenida vai até o semáforo localizado perto da loja Donna Donno.

Para evitar transtornos, a autarquia orienta os motoristas a usarem a Orla ou a Avenida das Nações como rotas alternativas. Quem precisar transitar entre Petrolina e Juazeiro deve fazer a travessia antes das 16h ou apenas depois do fim do evento.

O tráfego será organizado por agentes da AMMPLA, com apoio da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) e de policiais do Batalhão Integrado Especializado (BIEsp).

articles.title: Gastos de campanha com Meta chegam a recorde de R$ 289 milhões em 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Dona do Instagram, Facebook e WhatsApp, a Meta é a empresa que mais recebeu recursos das campanhas eleitorais até o momento. Entre os candidatos, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) foi quem mais declarou gastos com a plataforma, em um valor quase três vezes superior ao informado por Lula (PT), segundo as prestações de contas parciais das campanhas.
articles.summary: Os gastos de campanhas com Meta em 2026 somam R$ 289 milhões, valor recorde que representa mais que o dobro do total investido nas eleições de 2022.
articles.body:
Em 2026, a empresa que mais recebeu recursos das campanhas eleitorais foi a Meta. Segundo levantamento do g1 , os candidatos gastaram pelo menos R$ 288,7 milhões para contratar os serviços diretamente com a plataforma.

As informações foram obtidas por meio da prestação de contas presente nos dados abertos do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) e no DivulgaCand, plataforma do TSE com gastos dinâmicos da eleição.

Os dados de 2026 são parciais, já que o prazo para prestação final de contas dos candidatos que participaram do 1º turno se encerra em 3 de novembro. Os que seguiram para o 2º turno têm até o dia 14 de novembro para declarar todos os gastos na eleição (Veja, ao final da matéria, como o levantamento foi feito).

Não é a primeira vez que a Meta lidera o ranking de maior fornecedora dos candidatos das eleições. A empresa é a que mais arrecada nas eleições desde 2022. O total de recursos recebidos em 2026, no entanto, é recorde.

Na comparação com a última eleição nacional, em 2022, o valor mais do que dobrou. Naquela disputa, os candidatos declararam R$ 129 milhões em gastos diretos com a Meta, dona do Facebook, WhatsApp e Instagram. Em relação a 2018, quando foram declarados R$ 22,7 milhões, o montante parcial de 2026 já é 1.171% maior.

Em 2018, a Meta recebeu 0,7% de todos os recursos gastos pelos candidatos nas campanhas eleitorais. Desde então, essa participação vem crescendo:

Em 2026, já representa 6% de todos os gastos declarados até o momento.

Os recursos destinados pelas candidaturas à Meta dizem respeito aos diferentes serviços prestados pelas plataformas, como, por exemplo, a verificação de contas, anúncios e impulsionamento de postagens.

O impulsionamento de conteúdo ganhou peso nos orçamentos. Ele passou de 2,5% do gasto total das campanhas em 2018 para 8,9% nos dados parciais de 2026.

🔎 O impulsionamento é o pagamento feito a plataformas digitais, como Instagram, Facebook e TikTok, para ampliar o alcance de publicações. Pela legislação eleitoral, apenas candidatos, partidos e coligações podem contratar o serviço para propaganda eleitoral .

➡️ As regras proíbem o pagamento a influenciadores para promover candidaturas, incluindo as chamadas "publis". Mesmo manifestações espontâneas de apoio a candidatos não podem ser impulsionadas ou monetizadas.

Quanto as campanhas eleitorais pagaram à Meta — Foto: g1

Gastos com a Meta nas campanhas eleitorais — Foto: g1

Entre os partidos, o PL é o que mais gas diretamente com a empresa desde 2022. Em 2026, já declarou R$ 63,7 milhões com a empresa, quase quatro vezes o que gastou na eleição nacional anterior.

Em seguida vem o PT, com R$ 37,9 milhões; PSD, com R$ 30,3 milhões; e União Brasil, com R$ 23,3 milhões. Em 2018, o topo era do PSD, com R$ 3,4 milhões.

Os partidos que mais gastaram com a Meta em 2026 — Foto: g1

Já entre as candidaturas individuais, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que disputa a presidência da República no 2º turno, é quem mais contratou diretamente com a Meta em 2026, com R$ 7,45 milhões. O valor é quase o triplo de seu adversário na eleição, Lula (PT), que declarou até o momento gastos de R$ 2,59 milhões com a empresa.

No comparativo das candidaturas durante os anos, em 2018 nenhum candidato passou de R$ 1 milhão gastos com a empresa. Em 2022, foram 4. Em 2026, com o levantamento ainda parcial, já são 24, no total de R$ 41 milhões gastos com estas candidaturas.

Os dados foram obtidos a partir de arquivos de despesas contratadas da prestação de contas de candidatos, no Portal de Dados Abertos do TSE, gerados em 18 de outubro de 2026. O levantamento também cruzou dados do DivulgaCand, plataforma do TSE, consultados na mesma data.

Para o cálculo das despesas, foram considerados apenas os pagamentos cujo fornecedor direto é o CNPJ 13.347.016/0001-17 (Facebook Serviços Online do Brasil Ltda).

Os valores estão em reais da época de cada eleição, sem correção pela inflação.

O valor considerado é um piso. Ficam de fora os gastos de diretórios partidários, anúncios pagos por apoiadores e pagamentos feitos por meio de agências de conteúdo ou publicidade, que aparecem no CNPJ destes terceiros.

Os gastos de 2026 são parciais. O número deve subir com a entrega das contas finais, cujo prazo ainda está em aberto.

Nesta segunda-feira (19), o ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze, do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), deu 24 horas para que a Meta comprove que cumpriu a decisão da Corte que determinou a adoção de medidas para garantir isonomia na distribuição de conteúdos políticos e na veiculação de anúncios eleitorais durante o segundo turno das eleições.

Tanto o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) quanto o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que disputam a Presidência no segundo turno, acionaram a Justiça Eleitoral contra a Meta sob argumento de que seus conteúdos de campanha têm sido prejudicados nas plataformas da empresa.

Também nesta segunda-feira, o corregedor-geral da Justiça Eleitoral, ministro Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva, proibiu o deputado Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) e o influenciador Pablo Marçal de republicar conteúdos já vetados pelo TSE, sob pena de multa de R$ 50 mil por publicação. O ministro também determinou que a Meta e o X suspendam o impulsionamento pago de conteúdos das contas dos dois até o fim do segundo turno.

articles.title: Judge leans toward extending halt on tree clearing at golf course where Trump says redesign should start ‘immediately’
articles.summary: The judge said the administration’s argument that the downing of hundreds of trees at the golf course was unrelated to Trump’s renovation plan wasn’t credible.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The judge presiding over a court fight involving President Donald Trump’s plans to redo a golf course on federal land indicated Monday that she plans to extend her order blocking the administration from chopping down more trees at the site. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said at the seven-hour hearing that she believes it’s likely necessary to extend her order because she has already found the government acted in “bad faith” when it abruptly chopped down over 400 trees at the course over the Columbus Day holiday weekend. She said she didn’t buy the administration’s arguments that the tree clearing was unrelated to Trump’s renovation plan, which he said should begin “immediately.” “I mean, there is no universe in which all of this just coincidentally happened at the same time. There just isn’t,” she said. Lawyers for the Justice Department had argued there was no renovation plan in place — a stance that Trump undermined Sunday on social media when he said he was “pleased to announce” the Interior Department and “famed Golf Course Architect, Tom Fazio, has developed a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site of the current East Potomac Golf Links, located in Washington, D.C.” Trump, an avid golfer, said the renovation would begin “on November 15th, when the old Course will be closed to play.” He stepped up the time frame in a post Monday morning ahead of the hearing, calling the suit seeking to preserve the current course “ridiculous.” “The experts at ‘Interior’ are allowed to do this First Class renovation ‘as of right.’ They do not need an approval. Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY!” he wrote. During the hearing, administration officials maintained they weren’t aware of any concrete renovation plan. “There is no plan to close the course,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told Reyes, characterizing Trump’s directive as something he would “like” to do. Acting National Park Service Director Jessica Bowron told Reyes that the first time she’d heard of the planned closure was in Trump’s post. “I don’t have any information on the referenced plan,” she testified. Interior Department chief of staff Gregory Wischer, asked the same question by the judge, also said that he was “not aware” of any work planned to begin Nov. 15. The plaintiffs, a preservation group and two Washington residents, allege Trump’s plan would change the character of the 100-year-old site, which consists of three courses for varying skill sets. They said Trump’s renovation would transform it into a single championship-style course. Trump told reporters Monday that the site is “old, tired, beaten up, it’s useless. It doesn’t do much business. We want to do something great for Washington. We’re going to basically build a better golf course. You can call it a renovation. It should be very simple. It’s something the Interior Department is allowed to do, absolutely. All they want to do is fix up their property.” Reyes cited Trump’s posts as potential evidence of bad faith on the government’s part. “We did not go from zero to ‘work is scheduled to begin immediately’ in 60 seconds,” she said. Trump blasted Reyes as a “crazed lunatic” in his post Monday morning. Reyes didn’t directly refer to the insult, but she said at the end of the hearing that she had gotten messages from her brother and mother, who were “freaking out” after they heard a CNN report that she had received death threats — something that often happens when Trump lashes out at a judge on social media. “That a federal judge is getting death threats over a golf course — I really don’t think that’s what the founders envisioned,” Reyes said. The Justice Department had argued in court filings over the weekend that Reyes, who was nominated by former President Joe Biden, should recuse herself from the case because she was biased and yelled at Justice Department attorneys during the last hearing. They contended that her “histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial.” Reyes denied the request in an order Sunday. She acknowledged that she had been “furious” with the administration for failing to make good on its promises it would let her know well in advance whether any major work was being done on the course. “So what happened? Not sudden onset bias,” she wrote. “Instead, the Government decided to remove over 500 healthy, non-invasive trees from East Potomac Golf Course. It waited until 4:55 p.m. on the Friday of a holiday weekend to give notice that it would begin removing trees within 15 hours. It removed nearly 430 trees in one day and would have destroyed hundreds more but for a rain delay.”

articles.title: JD Vance declines to endorse Netanyahu despite Trump's strong backing
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance said he will not weigh in on Israel's upcoming election after Trump threw his support behind Netanyahu's reelection bid.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's reelection bid, saying he intends to stay out of Israel's election despite President Donald Trump throwing his support behind the Israeli leader. During an interview Monday with Mark Halperin on "2WAY Tonight," Vance said his focus remains on U.S. candidates ahead of the midterms, Politico reported. "The president has the most effective endorsement in American or international political history," Vance said. "I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on in the midterms. So I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections." OMAR RAID DRAWS OMINOUS WARNING FROM VANCE AS HE BLASTS PROGRESSIVE REP'S 'RAGE' TOWARD AMERICA However, Vance made clear that his decision should not be interpreted as opposition to Netanyahu. "I’m not anti-endorsing him. I’m not pro-endorsing him. I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections," the vice president added. The comments come one day after Trump gave Netanyahu his "Complete and Total Endorsement" in a lengthy Truth Social post, praising the prime minister as a key U.S. ally and partner in confronting Iran. "Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote. TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE Trump said Netanyahu had remained strong despite intense political pressure. "Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel. BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!" Trump said. Netanyahu quickly welcomed the president's backing, thanking Trump for what he called his "extraordinary endorsement." "President Trump, my friend Donald — thank you for your extraordinary endorsement," he said. "Israel has never had a greater friend in the White House. Together we will never let Iran's regime get nuclear weapons. Thank you for your clarity, courage and unwavering support." NETANYAHU PRAISES TRUMP'S 'WICKED SENSE OF HUMOR,' DEFENDS IRONCLAD ALLIANCE AHEAD OF HISTORIC ISRAEL VOTE Vance's decision to stay out of Israel's election comes after he reportedly waded into another foreign political contest earlier this year. The vice president previously traveled to Hungary in April, where he campaigned alongside then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban shortly before Orban lost his reelection bid, according to Politico. articles.title: Justice Department targets and charges 28 alleged noncitizen California voters
articles.summary: The Justice Department (DOJ) targeted and charged 28 alleged California voters who are not citizens, the department said in a press release Monday. The DOJ said in the press release that on Monday, federal authorities in California arrested 11 non-Americans residing in the country “who are among 28 total charged in criminal complaints with federal…
articles.body:
The Justice Department (DOJ) targeted and charged 28 alleged California voters who are not citizens, the department said in a press release Monday.

The DOJ said in the press release that on Monday, federal authorities in California arrested 11 non-Americans residing in the country “who are among 28 total charged in criminal complaints with federal crimes.”

The crimes, according to the DOJ, include fraudulently registering to vote in U.S. elections, with the majority of the 28 voting with “illegal and fraudulently obtained ballots.”

“Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen,” Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in the release.

“Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week,” he added.

The DOJ said in the release that each of the 28 hold green cards and “knowingly and willfully lied under oath” when filling out voter registration applications about having U.S. citizenship.

The Trump administration has cracked down intensely on immigration in President Trump’s second term, to much backlash. Federal immigration authorities have been involved in multiple incidents in which people have been wounded or killed since Trump’s return to the White House.

Last Thursday, the DOJ sued California after giving the state a USB drive and urging that within two days, it compare 20,000 names on its data rolls with information provided by the Department of Homeland Security.

The DOJ sent a letter to Golden State and local elections officials last Tuesday, warning of legal action if they didn’t compare the data. Per a copy of the letter provided by Los Angeles County, it included a handwritten password for the files on the drive.

articles.title: Elissa Slotkin calls backlash to threat of prosecution comments 'manufactured outrage'
articles.summary: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., dismissed criticism on CNN as "manufactured outrage" after her viral remarks about prosecuting Trump administration enablers.
articles.body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., called the backlash against her comments that the threat of prosecution could deter young people from working for the Trump administration "manufactured outrage" during television interviews Monday. During an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event, Slotkin drew criticism after a clip went viral showing her saying she wants to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" President Donald Trump and push a "deterrence message" for young people. "I want young people coming out of school to say, ‘Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity.’ I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that,’" she said. "I want that deterrence message," Slotkin said. While speaking with CNN's Jake Tapper on Monday, Slotkin responded to a comment from Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, who wrote that it was "absolutely disgraceful" to "threaten young Americans for participating in politics and serving their country" with legal retribution. MIKE DAVIS: SEN SLOTKIN REVEALS HER INSIDIOUS SCHEME TO TARGET YOUNG CONSERVATIVES "Yeah, well, look, that’s manufactured outrage," Slotkin responded. "That’s his specialty. I think the thing that I’ve heard from my own Republican colleagues and peers, including interns and folks who work around the Hill who come to our events, they’ll tell you, 'I was worried. My parents were worried, you know. It’s really messy. I’m not sure what to get involved in.' Politics, in general, has become messy." "But, you know, when you’re being forced by this administration, for instance, to sign a contract that is given over to a company that Trump Jr. is on the board of, and you know that that’s a problem," she added. Slotkin then referenced her viral video from 2025, in which she and five other Democratic lawmakers urged military members to "refuse illegal orders." She claimed that in both circumstances she was only encouraging people to reject illegal activity. "My point is, do not get yourself involved in illegal activity," she said. "It’s the same thing I was talking about a year ago. Whether you’re the uniformed military or a civilian in government, if you’re being asked to do something by the president or his team, that’s illegal, you have a responsibility to reject that. That is my point, and that was the point I was trying to make." SLOTKIN SAYS DEMOCRATIC PARTY NEEDS 'NEW LEADERSHIP': 'OLD MODELS ARE NO LONGER WORKING' Fox News Digital reached out to Lee's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. The White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's previous comments on Slotkin. "That's a hell of a statement. Slotkin said that there should be prosecutions in order to scare people from going into politics. That's a Democrat and that's what they do. That's all they're good at — and you know what? That's why they're getting their a--es kicked," Trump said. Slotkin reiterated that she had no intention of targeting people for prosecution solely because of their political affiliation and only cared about people "breaking the law." "If you are violating the law, then you should be held accountable, and that includes people who are supporting that activity. That’s the point I was trying to make. You’re not breaking the law? No problem. We can have disagreements all day long, and certainly Democrats and Republicans do. I don’t care if it’s just freedom of speech. I care if you’re breaking the law," Slotkin told CNN. PENNSYLVANIA SOCIALIST DEMOCRAT SAYS HE OPPOSES IMPRISONMENT EXCEPT FOR 'LAWLESS MAGA THUGS' During a separate interview on MS NOW, Slotkin suggested some of the backlash she received from Republican critics could be attributed to her gender. "I think when you choose to call out their corruption, they clearly don't like that," Slotkin said on MS NOW's "Deadline: White House." "They're clearly trying to change the conversation given what the midterms are and the state of the economy, the state of things around the country. I do think there's something about being a woman and criticizing them and calling them out on that corruption that really gets under their skin, obviously, or they wouldn't respond." articles.title: Trump uses antisemitic slur in defending Sen. Roger Marshall at rally in Kansas
articles.summary: Trump had used the term during a speech last year, leading to backlash. He said at the time that he wasn’t aware of the word’s antisemitic connotations.
articles.body: President Donald Trump used an antisemitic slur Monday in defending Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., after an article said he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid debts when he was a practicing physician. Speaking at a campaign rally in Kansas, Trump said the reporting made Marshall, who is not Jewish, out to be “some kind of a shylock-type guy,” using a term widely recognized as offensive toward Jewish people. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks. Trump used the same slur last year in a speech to describe exploitative bankers as he was promoting his sweeping domestic policy bill. Some Jewish groups denounced his use of the term. “Shylock” is a Jewish character in William Shakespeare’s play “The Merchant of Venice” sometimes called a usurer. The Anti-Defamation League, in a guide for educators teaching the play, says, “Shylock, and by extension, all Jews, are presented as money-hungry, conniving, and cruel.” Trump at the time denied having knowledge of the antisemitic connotations of the term, saying he had “never heard it that way” and adding, “To me, shylock is somebody that’s a moneylender at high rates.” Former President Joe Biden faced backlash in 2014 for using the word, which he later apologized for. Marshall, an obstetrician-gynecologist, faced backlash after The New York Times reported last month that he sued more than 700 patients for unpaid bills, which resulted in scores of arrest warrants for missed court dates. His lawyer said Marshall had no involvement in the warrants or the arrests, and Marshall called the story a “hit job.” “You got screwed with that stuff,” Trump said Monday about the reporting, addressing Marshall onstage. He did not mention the Times by name. Marshall, who has represented Kansas in the Senate since 2021, faces Adam Hamilton in a closer-than-expected race. Hamilton is a megachurch pastor and former Republican who said he decided to run as a Democrat this year after having considered a bid as an independent. Hamilton has picked up a number of endorsements from influential Republicans and Democrats in the state. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report characterizes the race as a “toss-up.” NBC News lists it as competitive but leaning toward the GOP.
