articles.title: Rogers warns Michigan voters against El-Sayed’s ‘extreme’ agenda ahead of election
articles.summary: Mike Rogers warned Michigan voters against Abdul El-Sayed’s agenda while touting his campaign’s momentum during a town hall with Sean Hannity.
articles.body: Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers took aim at Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed during a town hall with Fox News host Sean Hannity on Monday, warning voters that his rival's policies would hurt the state. Rogers accused El-Sayed of having a "pattern of deception" and called him a "manufactured candidate," claiming the Democrat has misrepresented his political positions. "He is the most extreme candidate. He has called for defunding the police. He has called for letting criminals out of prison," Rogers said. TRUMP TAKES BORDER CRACKDOWN TO DEEP-RED STATE AS SHOCK SENATE BATTLE THREATENS GOP STRONGHOLD "He has called for the Green New Deal, which for Michigan is a killer." Rogers also touted his campaign's ground operation, saying volunteers are approaching 6 million doors knocked across Michigan. "That's the energy, and what we're getting off of those doors is, 'Yes, we're voting,' 'No, we're not going to be a DSA state,' 'No, we're not going to let this happen on our watch.'" The Republican also said his campaign is seeing support from voters who traditionally back Democrats. MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT CONFIRMS SISTER-IN-LAW'S TERROR WATCHLIST LAWSUIT DAYS BEFORE OBAMA CAMPAIGN APPEARANCE Rogers later took questions from voters, including a Jewish woman who said she sometimes feels afraid to show her Jewish identity in public. Rogers said he had heard similar stories from Jewish students at the University of Michigan who said they concealed religious symbols because they were being harassed. Rogers also pointed to housing, education and skilled trades, saying he wants to make it easier for young adults to buy homes and bring more defense industry work to the state. 'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS DEFEND EL-SAYED COMPARING HIMSELF TO JFK OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SCRUTINY He also called for putting shop classes back in Michigan high schools, arguing that expanding skilled-trade education would give students more paths to well-paying careers. articles.title: Trump announces $8B relief program for farmers
articles.summary: President Trump announced Monday that a new $8 billion program will help provide temporary relief to farmers during the harvest season. Trump announced the Harvest Fuel Relief Program during his rally in Kansas stumping for GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, who is running for reelection in a competitive race against his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton. He…
articles.body:
President Trump announced Monday that a new $8 billion program will help provide temporary relief to farmers during the harvest season.

Trump announced the Harvest Fuel Relief Program during his rally in Kansas stumping for GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, who is running for reelection in a competitive race against his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton.

He said the $8 billion is “in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season.”

“Roger Marshall is the leader who fought for that to happen,” he said. “Roger got it to happen.”

The $8 billion will be available for one-time payments to farmers, a release from the Agriculture Department said.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said the program will deliver “critical support to farmers facing rising costs and market disruptions.”

Farm state Republicans have been pushing for the administration to do something about the high diesel prices amid the war with Iran.

The current average price for diesel is roughly $6.32 per gallon, according to AAA . The average price a year ago for diesel was $3.63 per gallon.

Trump has also tried other initiatives to lower high diesel costs. Earlier this month, he announced steps to increase the availability of red-dyed diesel .

The diesel has red dye added to it to signal that it is tax exempt. It’s typically used in farm and construction equipment.

While some Republicans have called for a pause to diesel exports, Trump said earlier this month that he would not authorize an export ban on diesel.

“We were never going to do it,” he told reporters earlier this month.

articles.title: Vance declines to endorse Netanyahu after Trump offers full support for re-election
articles.summary: Vance, who campaigned for ousted Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán this spring, said he endorses American candidates.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday, a day after President Donald Trump publicly backed Netanyahu as he seeks re-election this month. “I’m not getting involved in the Israeli elections,” Vance said in an interview on Mark Halperin’s show “2WAY Tonight.” “I’m not anti-endorsing him; I’m not pro-endorsing him,” Vance added. Trump weighed in on the election Sunday, strongly backing Netanyahu’s re-election bid. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so. Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that the post represents his “Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu.” Vance said Monday that Trump has “the most effective endorsement in American or international political history.” He further defended his refusal to get involved in the race by saying he endorses “American candidates,” adding “that’s what I’m focused on” as the midterm elections approach. Vance traveled to Hungary this year to stump for then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who was voted out of power in April after 16 years. Vance also reiterated Monday that he has not decided whether he will run for president in 2028. But should he do so, Vance said, he thinks Trump will endorse him. “I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028. I just haven’t focused on it,” Vance said. “I think if I run, the president will endorse me right away, right at the beginning.”

articles.title: Trump warns Kansans that US will 'burn' like France if Democrats win
articles.summary: PARK CITY, Kansas, Oct 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Monday used violent unrest in France as an argument against Democrats in his battle to def...
articles.body:
PARK CITY, Kansas, Oct 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Monday used violent unrest in France as an argument against Democrats in his battle to defend a Kansas Senate seat long held by Republicans but in danger of falling to his political opponents.

Trump's rally on behalf of Republican incumbent Roger Marshall was his latest ‌foray into conservative states where Republican candidates are on defense due to voter frustrations over the Iran war and rising prices.

"I love you Kansas, but I'm here for a guy named Roger ‌Marshall," Trump said.

In a new addition to his stump speech, Trump pointed to widespread protests in France as a scenario that could erupt in the United States unless Republicans win. He provided no evidence.

France in recent days has seen some of the worst unrest ​in years as huge protests over the cost of living and underfunded public services descended into riots and looting.

Trump himself has struggled to make goods and services more affordable in the United States.

In his speech, Trump turned to anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim rhetoric, the type that he used to fuel his three presidential campaigns.

"We're not going to let that happen to this country," he said. "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America."

Trump has been mocking Democrats by calling them Dumocrats. Rights advocates have repeatedly criticized Trump for his rhetoric over the years in which he has targeted and mocked immigrants and ethnic ‌minority groups. Civil rights groups say such rhetoric normalizes discriminatory attitudes towards ⁠those communities.

Kansas, a conservative Midwestern state Trump won by 16 points in 2024, has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. First-term Senator Marshall is in a close fight with Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, pastor of a Methodist megachurch, who is running against Trump's tariff agenda and what he calls the president's "erratic leadership."

"He ⁠wants you to repent for being born White," Trump said of Hamilton.

Marshall, in remarks to the rally, led his campaign argument on cultural issues like stopping "radical Islam." He called Hamilton "too woke" for Kansas because he supports gay pride parades, which the crowd loudly booed.

"We need someone who can sort heifers and steers," he said.

In response, Hamilton's campaign spokesperson called Marshall's campaign "sinking."

"Nothing said at the rally can distract from the fact Kansans are being crushed by rising gas and diesel prices, ​struggling ​to access affordable healthcare, and are tired of Washington corruption," the spokesperson, Tyson Brody, said.

In a Monday video, Hamilton welcomed ​Trump to the state and said his supporters have "a place" in his campaign. Hamilton said ‌he will work with Trump when it makes sense and stand up for Kansans when Washington policies hurt farmers and rural hospitals.

The tightness of the race is emblematic of the challenges looming for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections as they try to defy political headwinds and retain control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Trump is deep into a 32-day campaign blitz, frequently going to friendly areas that he won handily in previous elections.

One Republican familiar with Trump's midterm strategy said the president's attention on rural parts of the country is in response to internal polling showing soft support from men 55 years and younger in rural areas nationwide, a voting bloc crucial to Trump's 2024 presidential win.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, published on Monday, found that 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in office, a record low for the president.

Democrats need ‌a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and US Senate to overturn Republicans' narrow ​218-214 and 53-47 majorities.

In Park City, near Wichita, many rallygoers walked more than a mile across Interstate 135 to reach the rural ​arena, as a red-and-green truck stop sign flashed its latest prices above their heads: $3.98 for gas ​and $5.78 for diesel.

That is up about 45% compared to average gas prices in the state last year, according to motoring club AAA.

Economic concerns were palpable among Trump's most loyal ‌supporters.

"Being on disability, I don't have much, but it seems like the prices ​are still going up and they need to come down. ​It feels like you're having to search or hunt for food," said Monique Mullen, 59, a Republican voter from Hutchinson, Kansas, who takes care of her father.

A small bloc of protesters gathered near the arena, including James Nightingale, a self-described independent from Halstead, Kansas.

"I'm a farmer from Kansas and the Trump administration has decimated the farm economy in my area. Not only have his tariffs ​decimated our markets for grain sales, now he is bringing in imported beef ‌from outside the country. What happened to 'America First'?" he said.

Kansans have proven a willingness to cross parties, as voters have elected a Democratic governor, Laura Kelly, for the last two terms. "I ​don't think it's ever easy to get elected here," said Gina Seman, a Trump voter from Towanda, Kansas, noting that Republican candidates in the past have taken their popularity for granted.

(Reporting ​By Bo Erickson and Steve Holland; Additional reporting by Kanishka Singh; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title: Trump calls on New Mexico to change its name to ‘New America’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Monday called on New Mexico to change its name to “New America” — the latest example of him seeking geographical name changes that...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Monday called on New Mexico to change its name to "New America" — the latest example of him seeking geographical name changes that fit his political agenda.

"New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!" Trump wrote on Truth Social , shortly before departing the White House for a midterm rally in Kansas.

His comments about New Mexico — a blue state he lost by 6 points in 2024 — come as Republicans are anxious about holding their congressional majorities in November, with voters saying in polling that the president isn't paying enough attention to the country's most pressing problems.

Trump claimed, without citing any evidence, that "home values and incomes would rise" because of a name change. And he repeated his baseless claims about rigged elections by adding, "Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!"

Trump has previously suggested renaming New Mexico, although not so forcefully. In September, he posted to social media a map of the state with the word "Mexico" crossed out and "America" written underneath — an image that was reposted by the White House X account.

It's just the latest renaming push from Trump. He signed an executive order in August to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" as part of his ongoing trade war with Canada. He took similar action last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America." The president has also repeatedly floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz the "Trump Strait."

But while Trump has the power to rename what geographic landmarks, such as bodies of water, are called in the Geographic Names Information System, he doesn't have the constitutional ability to legally rename states. That process would need to happen within the state.

New Mexico's name predates the founding of the United States back to the 16th century, according to a fact sheet on the origin of state names from the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

New Mexico Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Monday evening dismissed Trump's comments.

"Let me repeat: New Mexico was New Mexico long before the United States existed and we'll be New Mexico forevermore," she wrote in a post on X .

Sen. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico wrote in a social post that the state's name "carries generations of history, culture, and rich traditions that continue to shape who we are."

"We are New Mexicans. We're proud of our name, proud of our home, and we're keeping both. Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we'll still be New Mexico," he continued.

This story has been updated with additional details.

CNN's Piper Hudspeth Blackburn contributed to this report.

articles.title: Senate Republicans might survive the blue thunderstorm. Uh, I think.
articles.summary: Democrats are talking confidently about a midterm wave, but Republicans are spending heavily to protect their Senate majority. From Susan Collins in Maine to the fight in Kansas, these races are anything but easy to call.
articles.body: With everyone and his brother predicting that a blue tsunami will wash over the Senate as well as the House, I want to write something contrarian. This way, if the Republicans do hang on to the Senate, I’ll get credit for defying the conventional wisdom. And if they don’t, I won’t get kicked out of the punditocracy – folks will just say well, he put a lot of caveats in there. THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND The truth is, I don’t know who is going to capture the upper chamber, and neither do you. And neither do all the pontificators and speculators online or on the air. I do know the GOP is pouring tens of millions into contests they might otherwise lose, giving their people – even scandal-scarred Ken Paxton – a huge advantage on the airwaves in the final two weeks. But money doesn’t always move voters once they’ve made up their minds in this era of early voting. Is Maine’s Susan Collins liked enough to hang one more time against aggressive Troy Jackson (and thankfully not weirdo Graham Platner), when Donald Trump shouts every day ‘Pretend I’m on the ballot’?" We got it, Mr. President. Josh Turek is an Iowa legislator and also a wheelchair basketball player who suffers from spina bifida. His GOP opponent, Rep. Ashley Hinton, says she doesn’t want "endless wars" but welcomes a Trump visit. Embed: She’s talked about such issues as open borders and transgender surgery. Turek has focused on the Iran war and soaring health premiums because Congress failed to amend the Affordable Care Act. In nearby Kansas, where Trump campaigned yesterday, Democrat Adam Hamilton is the founder of a Methodist mega-church, which would seem like a big plus in that conservative state, but some Dems are turned off by the religious aspect. Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, an obstetrician who served in the Army Reserves, was hurt by a New York Times report on him suing patients who were behind on their bills. By the way, did you ever think you’d see the day when the Republicans just gave up on North Carolina and steered their money elsewhere (conceding the win to former Gov. Roy Cooper)? PRESIDENT TRUMP HEADS TO KANSAS TO CAMPAIGN FOR SEN ROGER MARSHALL So I can conclude three things: Many of these races have 1-or-2 point "leads," which is within the margin of error, and polling is often inaccurate in an off-year election. The GOP is playing defense in ruby-red states–Trump in Kansas?—which is why Democrats are increasingly confident this is their big year. And, in the famous Tip O’Neill saying, all politics is local. There may be a mega-church guy or a man in a wheelchair or ex-Alaska congresswoman Mary Peltola, a former tribal judge who’s for "Fish, Family, Freedom," but who former staffers say they heard using awful slurs. How on earth do you handicap races with so many toss-ups? Of course, Republicans want to make the country believe that all Dems are like Michigan socialist Abdul el-Sayed, who, when asked whether he’d provide military aid if Israel was under attack, says he would rather spend the money at home. But (escape hatch here) I’m not saying it couldn’t happen.

articles.title: Rogers argues El-Sayed is vulnerable with 2 traditionally Democratic blocs as Obama heads to Michigan
articles.summary: Mike Rogers argues Abdul El-Sayed may lose Black and Jewish voters in Michigan's Senate race during a Sean Hannity town hall on key demographics.
articles.body: Republicans made their pitch to Michigan voters at a Fox News town hall Monday night, with GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers arguing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is vulnerable among Black and Jewish voters as one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races enters its final two weeks. Fox News host Sean Hannity also spoke with Republican gubernatorial nominee Rep. John James and House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., as the candidates sought to tie Michigan Democrats to government spending, socialism and the party's progressive wing ahead of Nov. 3. Early on in the night, Rogers argued that his opponent, El-Sayed, could underperform among a handful of key demographics that traditionally support Democratic candidates, presenting political opportunities for Republicans. Casting doubt on El-Sayed's grip on Black voters in Michigan EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PIKER, ISRAEL AND SOCIALIST TIES AFTER MIKE ROGERS SKIPS SENATE DEBATE Hannity pressed Rogers about El-Sayed's past criticism of former President Barack Obama, whom El-Sayed described as "not the right choice" to advance a progressive agenda following Obama's 2012 re-election. "He is dismissive in Detroit. We have just dozens of Black pastors that we have talked to, neighborhood leaders in the city of Detroit that we’ve talked to. They’re looking for a change," Rogers said. Notably, Obama is scheduled to campaign with El-Sayed in Detroit on Oct. 24 and has released a video urging voters to support the Democratic nominee. Unique opportunity for Republicans amid alienated Jewish voters ROGERS WARNS MICHIGAN VOTERS AGAINST EL-SAYED’S ‘EXTREME’ AGENDA AHEAD OF ELECTION Rogers argued the Jewish community could present a unique opportunity for Republicans amid El-Sayed's criticism of Israel. Recently, El-Sayed declined to answer whether he viewed Iran or Israel as a greater threat. "I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way. One, at risk of attacking us. One, getting us into wars we have no business fighting," El-Sayed said in a recent debate. Rogers noted that if only half of Jewish Democratic voters in Michigan felt alienated by El-Sayed’s remarks enough to support his campaign, it would provide a significant boost. "There are about 70,000 Jewish Democrats. If we get half of them to vote for us, which we think — we had an event last night. Had over 1,000 people at it. We’re fired up and excited and scared for their children, by the way. They’re afraid for their children. They’re with us, and they’re going to vote, we think, 35,000 votes out of the Jewish Democrat — these are normally solid Democratic votes." "That’s changing the dynamic," Rogers added. Gubernatorial hopeful promises to target fraud, trim fat on Democrat-led spending MINNESOTA FRAUD SCANDAL WILL HAUNT FLANAGAN IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE RACE, TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN WARNS Rep. John James, R-Mich., the state’s Republican candidate for governor, also appeared with Hannity, presenting his pitch to attendees on what he would do differently if elected. Alongside promises to reshape education, James promised to create more scrutiny around government programs and expenses. "Michigan is spending 50% more right now under Gretchen Whitmer than we spent under Rick Snyder’s administration, the last Republican, and $20 billion more per year than at the height of the pandemic." "Michigan does not have a taxation problem. Michigan has a spending problem," James added. Snyder left office in 2019. James also raised concerns about potential fraud in Michigan, drawing comparisons to Minnesota's sprawling taxpayer-funded fraud investigations. "If a 19-year-old journalist named Nick Shirley can find $9 billion of fraud in Minnesota, a state with 50% of our population and 60% of our budget, what do you think he can find here?" James said, referring to a videographer who had become famous for investigating Somali fraud rings. Shirley drew national attention to suspected fraud involving Minnesota childcare providers, although he did not uncover $9 billion in fraud. That figure came from former federal prosecutor Joe Thompson, who estimated last year that fraud across 14 high-risk Medicaid programs could total $9 billion or more. Minnesota officials have disputed the estimate. Federal and state investigators in Minnesota have uncovered fraud involving taxpayer-funded childcare, food assistance and healthcare programs, including schemes in which defendants allegedly billed the government for services they never provided. Top House Republican accuses Democrats of concealing 'Communist' agenda OBAMA'S STAR POWER GETS A REALITY CHECK FROM BLACK VOTERS IN CRUCIAL SENATE RACE: 'IT'S A TURNOFF' At the close of Hannity’s town hall, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., the House GOP conference chair, accused Democrats of hiding their true character. "I don’t even call them Democrats anymore; it’s the Communist Party," McClain said. "They want to pack the Supreme Court, they want to abolish the police, they want to let people out of prisons." articles.title: Navy robot deal quadruples as US looks to ‘outsmart’ China with AI at sea
articles.summary: Gecko Robotics unveiled its Komodo robot that scans warship decks like a CAT scan, mapping corrosion without stripping coatings for the U.S. Navy.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The U.S. Navy is quadrupling the ceiling on a contract for AI-powered robots used to inspect warships to $300 million. Just six months after initially tapping the technology to help get ships through maintenance and back to sea faster, the expanded agreement with Pittsburgh-based Gecko Robotics underscores the importance the U.S. military is putting on tech-based solutions. The initial ceiling for the deal was $71 million, but the Navy is pushing to improve fleet readiness amid a widening shipbuilding gap with China. "While the U.S. may not be able to out-manufacture faster than China, we can outsmart the ways that we maintain, operate and are ready with our vessels," Gecko Robotics CEO Jake Loosararian told Fox News Digital. Gecko says its technology can save the Navy up to $8 million in repair costs on a single ship and identify some structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional inspection methods. INSIDE TRUMP’S DEAL TO GIVE AMERICAN TAXPAYERS A MASSIVE STAKE IN NEW $6.6B SUBMARINE DEAL The company is also unveiling a new robot developed specifically for the Navy that can inspect the steel beneath thick coatings on warship decks without first stripping them away. Dubbed Komodo, the robot scans a ship's deck to map corrosion and material thickness, giving maintenance crews a picture of what needs to be repaired before more invasive work begins. "It's essentially a CAT scan," Loosararian said. "You're basically understanding exactly what's going on." Traditionally, determining the condition of steel beneath a ship's non-skid deck coating can require removing material before crews know the extent of the problem. Komodo is designed to gather that information without first taking the surface apart. "The robots are able to actually understand what's wrong without having to take apart the ship to figure out what to fix," Loosararian said. In another example cited by Loosararian, an assessment that initially called for roughly 1,200 square feet of repair work was narrowed to about 300 square feet after robotic inspections provided a more precise picture of the damage. "You reduce and focus the kinds of repairs that you need," Loosararian said. "You're repairing less." CHINA’S LONG-TERM FINANCES ARE ALL WET AS BILL TO MAINTAIN HUGE NAVY COMES DUE IN 2031 The increased ceiling comes just six months after the Navy awarded Gecko a five-year, $71 million contract vehicle to expand the use of its robotic inspection technology across the fleet. Under the initial agreement announced in March, Gecko was set to begin work on 18 ships in the U.S. Pacific Fleet, including destroyers, amphibious warships and littoral combat ships. The company's wall-climbing robots crawl across hulls, flight decks, ballast tanks and other difficult-to-access areas, scanning for corrosion, metal loss and other structural problems. The data is fed into Gecko's AI-powered Cantilever platform to help maintenance planners determine where repairs are needed. The goal is to find those problems earlier, before a ship enters a major maintenance period and crews discover additional work that can extend its stay in the shipyard. "The biggest savings are just in speed," Loosararian said. "Speed — you can't put a price tag on it, especially if you're in the U.S. Navy right now." The expansion comes as Navy leaders seek to push fleet readiness toward 80% while maintenance delays continue to sideline ships that would otherwise be available for deployment. China already fields a larger battle force than the U.S. Navy and can produce vessels at a pace American shipyards cannot easily match. That has put additional pressure on the Pentagon to keep more of the ships already in the American fleet available for operations. For Gecko, the longer-term goal is to move beyond finding existing damage and use years of inspection data to anticipate problems before they force ships into longer repair periods. "You are able to predict exactly what's going to break before it does," Loosararian said, allowing maintenance planners to have workers, materials and repair plans ready when a ship reaches the pier or enters a shipyard. The technology could also reduce the amount of dangerous and labor-intensive inspection work performed by shipyard workers as the industrial base struggles with shortages of skilled labor. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Loosararian said the combination of robotics and AI is ultimately aimed at allowing a limited workforce to spend more time fixing ships and less time determining what needs to be fixed. For a Navy racing to keep pace with a rapidly expanding Chinese fleet, he argued, getting more out of the ships already in the water could prove just as important as building new ones. "While the U.S. may not be able to out-manufacture faster than China," Loosararian said, "we can outsmart the ways that we maintain, operate and are ready with our vessels."

articles.title: Top Trump ally warns Republican Party 'dead' if it loses key voting bloc ahead of midterms
articles.summary: A top Senate Republican warns the GOP could be "dead as a party" if working-class voters abandon Republicans over economy and gas price woes.
articles.body: A top Senate Republican warned that the same voting bloc that has propelled the GOP to power over the last decade is at risk of turning its back on the party during this election cycle. For decades, White, working-class voters often aligned themselves with the Democratic Party, giving Democrats a stranglehold on Congress until the 1990s and often favoring the Democratic candidate atop the presidential ticket. President Donald Trump’s entrance onto the political scene and victory in 2016 solidified a shift that was years in the making, giving Republicans a strong base of working-class support. But with the state of the economy, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, a top ally of Trump’s on Capitol Hill, warned that the GOP’s steady base could head for the exits. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS "This is the whole deal," Moreno told Fox News Digital. "It's the whole deal. If we don't hang on to those working-class voters, we're dead as a party. That's why I say with no hyperbole, if President Trump hadn’t won in 2016, the Republican Party would be dead. Because the Republican Party had abandoned working-class Americans." "Ironically, the Democrats abandoned working Americans, and there was a void — President Trump filled it," he continued. "That's why he won." Trump has consistently performed highly with White, working-class voters each time he has run for office, scoring between 66% and 67% of their vote between 2016 and 2024, according to a variety of exit polls. REDISTRICTING GIVES REPUBLICANS AN EDGE, BUT AFFORDABILITY WILL DECIDE THE MIDTERMS Some Democrats acknowledged that after the 2024 election, their party had a problem with engaging the working class. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., circulated a memo that urged Democrats to embrace economic populism following stunning losses across the gamut of power in Washington. "No one, including me, has all the answers right now, but what we know for certain is that Democrats must reclaim our identity as the party of the working class," Murphy wrote. Still, Republicans are facing political headwinds heading into this midterm election cycle, in which affordability issues are dominating headlines and voters’ concerns. FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS Trump and the GOP again rose to be the dominant party in Washington, D.C., after the 2024 election by pitching a message to rectify the economy that the president charged was "destroyed" by former President Joe Biden. But a Fox News poll published earlier this month found that nearly 60% of voters said that their top concern was the economy. A separate Fox News poll published in May found that 67% of White voters without a college degree disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy. Republicans have hit the trail this fall pitching their economic successes, particularly from the colossal "big, beautiful bill" and trying to instill in voters that the cost of fuel, for example, is only temporary as the war with Iran continues. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Moreno, however, argued that working-class voters "hate" the war. "They obviously hate gas prices because, look, they're already struggling. I mean, you talk to some of these working Americans, they're an engine failure in their vehicle away from bankruptcy, and that's a disaster." "So, I think what we have to do is explain, this is a very, very necessary thing that had to happen," he continued. "Iran was attacking us for 47 years, and we didn't take him out. They would have used a nuclear weapon. I don't know that that case is penetrated enough, and this gas price situation will be very temporary."

articles.title: Ilhan Omar's sister questioned by feds after dramatic DC home raid
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar's older sister Sahra Noor was questioned by federal investigators in connection with the immigration fraud probe following the DHS raid.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Rep. Ilhan Omar's older sister was questioned by federal investigators last week in relation to an immigration fraud probe into the congresswoman, Fox News Digital has learned. Three sources familiar with the investigation said Sahra Noor voluntarily spoke with the investigators after the high-profile Monday morning raid on the residence Omar shares with her husband in Washington, D.C. It is not clear the scope of the conversation Noor had with investigators. Like Omar, Noor came to the United States as a child fleeing the civil war in Somalia. She currently lives in Kenya, according to her LinkedIn page, but has been in the United States promoting her new book, "Salt in the Snow: A Somali Immigrant Story." The House lawmaker's sister canceled a Minnesota stop on the book tour last week amid the fallout of the raid and the ensuing interview with authorities. ILHAN OMAR'S SISTER SKIPS BOOK TOUR EVENT AMID WEEK OF CHAOS FOLLOWING RAID ON PROGRESSIVE'S DC HOME The book event, which was scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at the University of Minnesota Rochester, was promoted online by Garden Party Books, a local bookstore that listed itself as a "proud supporter" of the event alongside the university and the Rochester Public Library. A representative from Garden Party Books told Fox News Digital last week that the event was canceled because Noor had a "family emergency." It is now revealed that last week she was questioned by federal investigators. Omar’s D.C. home was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigatory body of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), at around 6 a.m. last Monday. Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the agency executed a search warrant in relation to an immigration fraud probe. Specifically, they are probing whether the lawmaker or her father falsified information when filling out her citizenship paperwork. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS Border czar Tom Homan revealed over the weekend that if the allegations are proven, they could lead to Omar’s denaturalization. During the raid, Omar’s personal phone, passport and computer were seized, The Wall Street Journal reported last week. And Omar’s attorneys over the weekend demanded that the Justice Department return some of the property confiscated by HSI. Additionally, The New York Times reported that about a dozen people, including Omar’s relatives, have been subpoenaed in the case. Omar has not been seen publicly since before the raid, though her husband has been seen several times walking their dog, taking out the trash and speaking outside the home with one of the congresswoman's aides. Omar has not responded to Fox News Digital's repeated requests for comment, but she did react to the raid publicly on social media. "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," she said in a statement posted to X hours after feds descended on her home. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE "For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," the post continued. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies." In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital last Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance said the investigation is not politically motivated. "We don't want to be like the Biden administration. We never want to be like that — where they would allow the law to go after their political opponents," he said. DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ "We really want to let the law, the facts drive this," he continued. "And if justice requires something else be done, then, of course, we'll take a step when we have to." Fox News Digital reached out to Noor, but did not hear back before publication. articles.title: MORNING GLORY: Minnesota's massive fraud scandal could deliver a stunning Senate upset
articles.summary: Michele Tafoya's debate takedown of Peggy Flanagan over Minnesota's estimated $9 billion fraud scandal has reshaped the Minnesota Senate race.
articles.body: "This historic fraud happened under her watch, and suddenly, she’s looking out for Medicaid and SNAP? Sell it to someone else, Peggy." articles.title: Democratic super PAC hammers GOP over trans bathroom focus
articles.summary: A Democratic super PAC is hammering Republicans over their focus on transgender issues as GOP candidates in battleground races invoke culture war issues against their Democratic opponents in the final stretch of the midterm cycle. Progress Action Fund released a new ad on Tuesday, first shared with The Hill and part of an ad…
articles.body:
A Democratic super PAC is hammering Republicans over their focus on transgender issues as GOP candidates in battleground races invoke culture war issues against their Democratic opponents in the final stretch of the midterm cycle.

Progress Action Fund released a new ad on Tuesday, first shared with The Hill and part of an ad buy worth more than $1 million, that portrays a generic Republican congressman tasked with checking whether girls are using a bathroom that aligns with their biological sex.

In the 30-second ad called “Republicans In Your Bathroom,” a girl walks into a bathroom stall, screaming when she realizes a GOP congressman is waiting in the stall for her.

“I’m your Republican congressman,” the generic lawmaker says to the girl after she asks what he’s doing in the stall. “Now that we’re in charge, I’m checking to make sure there’s no trans people in the wrong bathroom.”

“Bathrooms are private. Don’t you have anything better to do?” she asks.

“I won the last election, and this is my priority,” the lawmaker replies. “Now, let’s make sure you’re really a girl.”

The ad is scheduled to air on connected TV and streaming services in Texas and Ohio two weeks out from Election Day. Both states are home to competitive Senate and House races that will determine the majorities in both chambers.

“Americans want their elected officials to lower gas prices and end the war in Iran, not follow them into the f–king restroom,” Progress Action Fund executive director Joe Jacobson said in a statement. “Republicans are creepy as hell. Democrats need to grow a spine and call Republicans out for their creepy fetish of monitoring children’s bathrooms.”

Republican candidates have leaned into transgender issues, particularly the debate into whether transgender girls and women can play on sports teams that align with their gender identity, as a major attack line against Democrats.

Republican Ken Paxton, who is facing off against Democrat James Talarico for the open Texas Senate seat, has attacked the state lawmaker in ads for his past comments on transgender issues, including for saying there’s more than two biological sexes and that he loves trans children.

A polling average of Texas Senate surveys compiled by Decision Desk HQ shows Talarico holds a narrow 2-point edge against Paxton, at 49 percent and 46.8 percent, respectively.

“I know there are two sexes, men and women. I also know there’s a very small percentage of people who have these chromosomal abnormalities, and I believe they deserve to be treated with dignity and respect,” Talarico told CBS News in May when asked about some of his past remarks.

Another Republican group has also attacked former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) over the issues of gender-affirming care and transgender individuals using the bathroom that aligns with their gender identity. Brown is locked in a tight battle against Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) in the Buckeye State.

A DDHQ polling average of Ohio Senate surveys shows Brown narrowly leading Husted by over a point. Brown sits close to 48 percent, while Husted sits at 46 percent.

Brown’s campaign responded with its own ad , in which several people, ostensibly Brown supporters, dismiss the attacks and ask why Republicans are focused on the transgender issue before attacking Husted over high costs of living.

articles.title: JB Pritzker is turning midterm money into potential 2028 leverage
articles.summary: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) may be trailing some of his potential 2028 Democratic presidential rivals in the early polling of the race. But as he mulls a White House bid, the billionaire governor is leading the midterms money war, pouring millions of dollars into Democratic campaigns. It’s a move that could pay political dividends for…
articles.body:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) may be trailing some of his potential 2028 Democratic presidential rivals in the early polling of the race.

But as he mulls a White House bid, the billionaire governor is leading the midterms money war, pouring millions of dollars into Democratic campaigns. It’s a move that could pay political dividends for him should he decide to run in 2028.

Pritzker has spent more than $38 million during the 2026 midterm cycle — including in battleground states like Michigan, Nevada and New Hampshire, which also happen to be three early-voting states on the Democratic calendar.

He has helped Democrats in red states too. Pritzker donated $100,000 to Lone Star Rising, a super PAC backing Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas.

Reuters reported last week Pritzker has also put in $65 million of his own money into his gubernatorial campaign, which he is expected to win handily.

Pritzker, who is worth an estimated $4.2 billion, is an heir to the Hyatt Hotels fortune and has long been one of the party’s biggest donors. And Democratic strategists say that financial advantage could help him build relationships and goodwill as he enters a Democratic primary.

“It doesn’t guarantee him support, but it guarantees people will give him a real listen if he decides to run,” said Steve Schale, the veteran Democratic strategist who led former President Obama’s campaigns in Florida. “It buys you a good list to start from, and you just want to build that list as large and as deep as you can. And for Pritzker, that’s a huge advantage.”

Democratic strategist Basil Smikle agreed, saying that it helps Pritzker to be “invested in Democratic victories that could create friendly territory in a primary.”

“For all those investments in specific districts or through groups doing work in specific areas, the association can create zones of familiarity and favor.”

But, Smikle added, “It doesn’t guarantee endorsements — especially early ones that help create distance from other candidates.”

While Pritzker has been the biggest checkwriter, other 2028 contenders have been throwing some financial weight behind various midterm efforts and candidates.

As of earlier this month, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) has raised $6.5 million for nearly all state parties, progressive groups and candidates just through his massive email list of small donors alone, one source close to the governor said.

Newsom has built the list over the last few years, and while the number of donors is unknown, it’s said to be among the largest in the Democratic Party, and something that will help boost Newsom’s prospects should he enter the race.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) — who is deciding if she’ll launch a White House bid or a race for the upper chamber, possibly against Senate Democratic Leader Charles Schumer (N.Y.) — last week donated $1 million to Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D), her largest donation this cycle.

Giving money to political candidates in a bid to create allies has been a tool used by other billionaires.

And while it can certainly help a candidate, there’s no guarantee of success.

Big donations didn’t help former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who spent more than $1 billion of his own money in 2020 but flamed out quickly in the Democratic presidential primary. It also didn’t ultimately serve California billionaire Tom Steyer (D), who invested $340 million into his campaign that same year.

“Mike Bloomberg and Tom Steyer spent more than a billion dollars between them in 2020 and didn’t win a single state,” said Democratic strategist Anthony Coley. “They’re proof that money can get you a microphone in a Democratic primary, but it can’t buy you the voters.”

“2028 will be a change election,” Coley added. “Voters will want a fighter with a compelling vision for where the country goes next, and the ability to connect, authentically, with people wherever they get their news. Money can help with that. But history says it’s only one part of the equation.”

Democratic strategist Brad Bannon said independent expenditure groups have changed the dynamics heavily for candidates.

“Being number one in personal fundraising is not as much as a boost as it used to be,” Bannon said. “One stroke of a keyboard could eliminate his financial edge in a flash.”

Still, he added, “It’s always better to be first in fundraising, like Pritzker is, than last.”

articles.title: Corruption charges once propelled MAGA. Now they may doom it
articles.summary: You can find the origins of the MAGA movement, now hurtling toward its rendezvous with the midterm electorate, in many places. The most obvious, straight-line antecedent is, of course, the Tea Party revolt of 2009 and 2010. The bipartisan backlash against the bailouts of Wall Street and Detroit fused with the conservative outrage at ObamaCare…
articles.body:
You can find the origins of the MAGA movement, now hurtling toward its rendezvous with the midterm electorate, in many places.

The most obvious, straight-line antecedent is, of course, the Tea Party revolt of 2009 and 2010. The bipartisan backlash against the bailouts of Wall Street and Detroit fused with the conservative outrage at ObamaCare became the dominant voice in Republicans’ wilderness era.

That was where Donald Trump joined the fray, latching on to the idea from the swamps of the suddenly very-online right, that then-President Obama was a stealth Kenyan — the Manchurian candidate, but for Islamism. You all know the story about how, at the moment when Trump succeeded in forcing Obama to release his birth certificate, the then-host of “The Celebrity Apprentice” attended the 2011 White House Correspondents’ Association dinner. Obama and headliner Seth Meyers roasted Trump repeatedly to the howling delight of the audience. Legend has it that Trump decided to run for president himself that night.

For a nice full-circle moment, watch the opening montage for Obama’s speech, which uses Hulk Hogan’s theme song “Real American” to mock lowbrow patriotism, and the use of the song to introduce the Hulkster himself endorsing Trump at the 2024 Republican National Convention. The Obamanauts no doubt believed they were actually mocking Trump’s own vulgar expressions of patriotism and xenophobia, but like a lot of late Obamism, it seemed pretty smug. And even if many of the Trumpsters were quietly LOL-ing at the yokels who unironically love pro wrestling like they love a Trump and Lee Greenwood-branded Holy Bible (still just $59.99) they weren’t letting it on to the marks.

It was 13 long years from the triumph of Obama (the birth certificate dinner was the same week he announced the killing of Osama bin Laden) to the political apotheosis of Trump in which he, having survived an assassination attempt just days earlier, took the stage at his Hulkamaniac nominating convention in 2024. And propelling it all was the same kind of rage that had given the Tea Party its start: the belief among many “real Americans” that the game was rigged against them and that Trump, whom Dave Chappelle famously called “ an honest liar ,” would help tear it all down.

Another, less remembered forerunner of MAGA was Ross Perot’s 1992 presidential candidacy and the Reform Party it birthed. That was actually where Trump first dipped his toes into presidential politics, with a short-lived campaign for the party’s 2000 nomination. If you’ve never read Matt Labash’s dispatch from the abortive Trump effort, do yourself a favor . The idea is that Trump was a logical heir to fellow businessman Perot: a candidate too rich to buy and too famous to be silenced.

It was in the zeitgeist back then, when the whiff of Iran-Contra was still in the air, campaign finance reform was a hot issue and the scandals of Bill Clinton, ranging from the slightly sordid to the outright sleazy, had dominated political news from the time he launched his candidacy to his final day in office. Perot had a lot of way-out ideas, but the central argument of his candidacies was that Washington had been overrun by lobbyists and special interests and that he would set things right.

“​If someone as blessed as I am is not willing to clean out the barn, who will?” Perot liked to say. It’s a far cry from Trump’s “ I am your retribution ,” but there’s some overlap there: the big man, the outsider, the hard edge, the unlikely savior. Perot was playing it like Marshal Will Kane, while Trump was doing more of a Tony Soprano take, but the idea of the tough guy, willing and able to do hard and necessary things, has always been very appealing to Americans concerned about the accumulation of power by remote elites.

In his first term, Trump leaned into that persona. He made a show of announcing which government agency would be getting the proceeds of his presidential paycheck — veterans, schools, health programs, infrastructure, the National Park Service etc. In the second term, I could find only one such announcement: a claim in August of last year that his paycheck was going to White House renovations .

Similarly, he went to great lengths in the first term to at least pay lip service to ethical restrictions on his and his family’s business activities during the presidency. It’s not that he or they followed those rules to the letter, but, as the saying goes , “hypocrisy is the tribute that vice pays to virtue.” Critics may have scoffed at Trump’s claims that he was giving up greater wealth and comfort to serve, but for those inclined to believe him in the first place, it was a pretty good pitch. When Democrats came after Trump for penny-ante stuff like profiting from the hotel stays of foreigners seeking favor with the administration, it didn’t land.

But in Trump 2.0, hypocrisy was out and brazenness was in. The billions Trump has raked in, the obsession with an opulent ballroom for the White House, lavish gifts from abroad and the government contracts for his family were bad enough, but probably the most damaging politically has been that at a moment when Americans are extremely anxious about the coming disruptions from artificial intelligence, Trump is enthusiastically on the same team as the other billionaires. As with the unfulfilled promises in the Jeffrey Epstein probe, Trump no longer seems to be leading the angry mob, but instead deflecting its rage.

Many were surprised to see that in the most recent Fox News poll , corruption was a top concern for 90 percent of voters, ahead of even high prices. They shouldn’t have been shocked. There are two main flavors of American populism: economic and cultural. What unites them is the belief that the system is rigged against their interests. If Trump has put his party on the wrong side of the mob he once led, there will be hell to pay next month.

Stirewalt is the politics editor for The Hill, veteran campaign and elections journalist and best-selling author of books about American political history.

articles.title: The Memo: Trump plan for golf course becomes battle over court’s power
articles.summary: A battle over a Washington golf course has turned into a fiery showdown over the powers of the Trump administration to do as it wishes and the power of the courts to constrain it. At issue is the East Potomac Golf Links, an unglamorous but busy municipal course roughly 2 miles from the White House.…
articles.body:
A battle over a Washington golf course has turned into a fiery showdown over the powers of the Trump administration to do as it wishes and the power of the courts to constrain it.

At issue is the East Potomac Golf Links , an unglamorous but busy municipal course roughly 2 miles from the White House.

Trump wants to redevelop the course into a sleeker, professional course capable of hosting top-level tournaments.

But doing that, in his mind, requires the cutting down of hundreds of trees — which has already taken place, much to a judge’s fury.

Plans posted by Trump on social media on Sunday appear to also call for the destruction of a roadway around the small peninsula that the golf course dominates. The roadway is particularly popular with cyclists and runners. Adjacent picnic areas draw Washingtonians especially in the summer months.

Even before Trump’s latest social media posts, conservation groups and individual golfers have sought to prevent Trump from moving ahead.

The judge in the case, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes, has sought to pause major work on the course while the underlying case proceeds.

Reyes plainly does not believe the administration had respected her orders. The administration seems, basically, of the opinion that it doesn’t have to.

A week ago, White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller wrote on social media , “A federal judge has no jurisdiction whatsoever over the maintenance of this course.”

Early Monday morning, right before a fresh hearing on the matter, Trump declared the judge “a crazed lunatic” in a social media post in which he also mused whether she “may be insane?”

The mayhem just underscores the manner in which the case has become about something much more important than the fate of a golf course.

“At a time when our country is at war and everyone is worried about the economy and high prices, the President simply doesn’t care,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) wrote on social media on Sunday. “He’s focused on building an upscale golf course within walking distance of the White House. And on his fancy ballroom and his memorial arch to himself.”

The case came to national attention more than a week ago, when more than 500 trees were chopped down . Video clips that went viral on social media captured many of the trees being felled, fueling the rage of Trump critics who saw the move as emblematic of his general penchant for unilaterally remaking Washington .

The destruction of the trees also infuriated the judge, who in essence accused the administration of defying her earlier requests to be kept informed in advance of any proposed major changes to the course.

She complained that the government’s actions had caused it to lose “all of its credibility with me in this case.” She also declared herself “thoroughly unamused” by the government’s actions. A New York Times report of that hearing last week noted that the judge “raised her voice at several points to near shouting level.”

Things have only devolved further from there.

A Friday filing from Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward sought Reyes’s recusal, asserting among other things that she had “allowed her disdain for the Trump Administration to influence how hearings unfold” and that her “behavior in this case is nothing short of egregious.”

On Sunday, the judge declined to recuse herself, in an indignant ruling that quoted liberally from previous hearings in the matter. Reyes, nominated to the District Court bench by former President Biden, suggested the administration was trying “to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion” and added that “by any objective measure, the Government fails to meet the standard for recusal.”

Harry Litman, a former U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Pennsylvania, told this column that the judge at this point was “representing the institutional power of the courts.”

Litman drew a parallel with U.S District Court Judge James Boasberg, who has tangled with the Trump administration over perceived disregard of orders he made halting deportation flights to El Salvador.

On Monday, Reyes created a stir at a new hearing by asking in open court whether other government lawyers were willing to sign on to a Sunday filing signed by Woodward alone.

The court filing contended that there was no “final” plan for the golf course despite Trump’s posting of the plans Sunday. In that post, the president stated that work would begin on the redesigned course on Nov. 15. His post included no suggestion that this would be dependent, in his mind, on clearance from the court.

Woodward further argued that the plans in any event did not amount to official “agency action” by the government, asserting: “Just as a decision to redesign all the art exhibits in a Smithsonian Museum would not be agency action, neither would a decision to redesign a golf course, or to trim trees, replace fences, expand the fairways, or mow the lawn.”

In relation to Reyes’s actions asking others in the court if they were willing to sign on to the filing, Litman argued, “She is very much trying to put space between the normal, professional staff of the DOJ and the political cadre that presumably takes orders from Donald Trump.”

“I see it as an increasingly number of courts being suspicious or skeptical or willing to rule against” the administration, he added.

Monday’s hearing did not produce an immediate ruling.

Plainly, Trump is not for stopping. The question is whether Reyes will force a halt regardless.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Mark Kelly climbs ranks of Democratic hopefuls, as he barnstorms country
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) is climbing the ranks of potential 2028 Democratic White House hopefuls as he travels extensively around the country this year to meet voters and raise millions of dollars for Democratic candidates in key battleground states. Kelly will have campaigned for Democratic candidates in nearly 20 states by the end of the…
articles.body:
Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) is climbing the ranks of potential 2028 Democratic White House hopefuls as he travels extensively around the country this year to meet voters and raise millions of dollars for Democratic candidates in key battleground states.

Kelly will have campaigned for Democratic candidates in nearly 20 states by the end of the midterm election cycle, making valuable voter and donor contacts in an array of pivotal states, such as Arizona, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina and Virginia.

Several of those states are not only key Senate battlegrounds but they will also be important presidential battlegrounds in the next election cycle.

And several of those states will be early Democratic primary states.

South Carolina will host the first Democratic presidential primary contest on Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada on Feb. 1, New Hampshire on Feb. 8, New Mexico on Feb. 15, Michigan on Feb. 22 and Virginia on Feb. 29.

Kelly told The Hill in an interview Monday that he’s getting closer to making a decision about running for president but won’t do so until “the other side of this election.”

The senior senator from Arizona said he never envisioned himself running for Senate until a woman from Phoenix pleaded with him to run for the upper chamber the night before Election Day 2018 because she feared her son with Down syndrome was about to lose his healthcare coverage.

He said Republican colleagues in Washington “are missing the frustration out there.”

“Folks can’t afford their lives anymore, people getting kicked off of Medicaid and SNAP [Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program], rent prices are up, young people don’t really consider buying a home now until their 40s. I bought my first house when I was 28, I was in the Navy,” he said.

Kelly this week will host a series of events across Arizona for the 18 state legislative candidates he’s endorsed to help Democrats flip the state legislature.

On Thursday and Friday, he will travel to Arizona and campaign with Democrats up and down the ballot.

He will spend the weekend in New Mexico, where he and his wife, former Rep. Gabby Giffords (D-Ariz.), will speak at a rally sponsored by Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and campaign with Deb Haaland, the Democratic nominee in New Mexico’s gubernatorial race.

Kelly, who was on former Vice President Kamala Harris’s short list of possible running mates in 2024, seems poised to take a prominent role in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary.

“I think he’ll be an incredibly formidable candidate for president if he decides to run. He has the temperament, the background, the experience and the proven ability to win states in a battleground state — not to mention his incredible relationship with his wife who has been through so much,” said Tad Devine, a Democratic strategist who worked on Al Gore’s 2000 presidential campaign, former Sen. John Kerry’s (D-Mass.) 2004 presidential campaign and Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-Vt.) 2016 presidential campaign.

A major part of Kelly’s life story is his marriage to Giffords, who was shot and severely injured in 2011. They later founded Americans for Responsible Solutions to address gun violence.

Kelly said earlier this year he will “seriously consider” a presidential run.

His credentials as a combat-tested Naval aviator and demeanor as a sharp and sober-minded senator appear well-matched to what voters may be looking for in a successor to President Trump, Democratic strategists and political experts say.

“That is a guy who would be taken very seriously by voters if he decides to run for president,” Devine said.

Kelly has played a prominent role speaking out on national security issues during Trump’s second term.

His pointed criticisms of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — over Hegseth’s use of commercial messaging app Signal to discuss sensitive military operations, and over the Pentagon’s rapid consumption of missiles and other high-value munitions during the first weeks of the Iran war — have stood out.

Kelly told The Hill on Monday that Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution of Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan is the latest evidence he’s unfit to lead the Defense Department.

“I think Hegseth should have been fired multiple times, on multiple occasions. The last time he should have been fired when he called for a public execution. I mean, seriously? In the United States, start publicly executing people?” he said. “That’s not who we are. That fundamentally changes the character of this country if we do it.”

Kelly made his biggest splash in the national media under Trump by recording a video with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and several House Democrats urging military service members to disobey illegal orders.

More than anything, the backlash from the Trump administration to that video put Kelly at the center of a big national story and raised his prominence with Democratic donors, activists and voters.

Hegseth censured and tried to demote Kelly in rank and reduce his retirement pay but was blocked by a federal district court judge.

The Trump Justice Department attempted to charge him and other Democrats with seditious conspiracy, but a federal grand jury declined to indict them.

Kelly emphasizes in media appearances that he has a different background than any other Democrat who is looking at running for president in 2028.

“I spent 25 years in the Navy, 15 at NASA. I was a combat pilot in the first Gulf War. I have a background in engineering,” Kelly told ABC15, a local Arizona television station last month.

“Most of the folks up here come from some other background. There are a lot of lawyers. I have to figure out what the country needs here as we turn the corner and turn the page on this disaster of an administration,” he said of his colleagues in both chambers and of governors who are eyeing a presidential bid in the coming months.

Steve Jarding, a longtime Democratic strategist, said he “easily” puts Kelly in the top five most promising potential Democratic presidential candidates in 2028.

He argued Kelly’s background as a combat veteran and astronaut makes him stand out in a field of Democrats that could include Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.) and fellow Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.).

“I rank him very high,” Jarding said, citing “his background, his record, the military stuff, which I think is important for the Democrats to get the Department of Defense back under control … he would certainly be a voice who could do that.”

“I would put him easily in the top five, if not the top two or three. His profile would be hard to beat,” he added. “He checks a lot of boxes.”

Kelly has so far raised about $14.1 million for Democrats this election cycle, including $4.1 million for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and more than $3 million for the Democratic National Committee.

Democratic strategists say the contacts Kelly is making in early Democratic presidential primary states will pay off if he launches a run for president next year.

“It’s critical because in those early states you have to make relationships actually with people, real human beings who are key people within their states. And the only way to do that is to go there, spend time with them, get to know them and get them to come out for you early,” Devine, the former Democratic presidential strategist, explained.

Kelly’s also picking up insights from frustrated voters, such as a group of business owners in Yuma, Ariz., who met with him Monday.

He says the Trump economy is hitting people hard in unexpected ways.

Arizona has been hurt by the president’s ugly trade fight with Canada, along with his quips about making Canada the 51st state, because Canadian tourists have stopped coming south for the winter.

“I just met with some small business owners, and they are frustrated because Canadian tourists have stopped coming here. They used to benefit from Canadians in RVs [recreational vehicles] who would spend their winters here — hundreds, if not thousands, of them. And they would spend a lot of money,” Kelly said.

“One guy, I was at his restaurant today, he said that this has been harder than COVID for him,” the senator recounted. “It’s because how this president has insulted Canada. Canadians don’t come to vacation in the United States anymore, and they don’t want to buy our products when they’re even still on the shelves in Canada.”
