articles.title: Elissa Slotkin tells students like me not to work in government. Don’t listen to her
articles.summary: Elissa Slotkin's University of Chicago remarks targeted young conservatives considering Trump administration roles, raising the stakes for midterms.
articles.body: Last week, Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin came to the University of Chicago to send a message to young conservatives: stay out of government, or else. The visit came with little attention initially. Senator Slotkin chose her words carefully. She talked about fighting for the middle class, criticized President Trump’s economic policies and kept her name in the running for president in 2028. But, buried between her typical politician-speak, she made a clear threat towards young conservatives. Asked whether she wanted to impeach the president, she pivoted and spoke of effectiveness. She thought the 67-vote threshold for conviction in the Senate was too hard to meet, so instead the best course of action would be to go after the people around the president. That way, young people who may be interested in working in the Trump administration would say, "Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, so let me avoid participating in that." MIKE DAVIS: SEN SLOTKIN REVEALS HER INSIDIOUS SCHEME TO TARGET YOUNG CONSERVATIVES That threat felt personal to me. When I was in high school, I served as a United States Senate page. For those unfamiliar with the program, it selects 30 juniors from across the country to spend a semester going to school and working in the Senate. I did my math homework on the Senate floor when Congress was out of session and ran around delivering messages and papers during session. I made many of my closest friends during that program, few of whom share my viewpoints on politics. And I gained a deep respect for the body I worked for. When I completed the program, my friends and family asked me whether I felt more optimistic or pessimistic about our government. The news coming out of Washington was so bad, they just assumed it would be pessimistic; they were interested in stories about senators yelling at one another and fighting to the death in meaningless partisan battles. But I came out of that program more optimistic than ever. Top of the list of reasons was that no matter their political allegiance, senators encouraged us — a group of impressionable high schoolers — to go into politics and make our voices heard. I was excited about the prospect that I could really make a difference in the future of our country. Hearing Senator Slotkin’s comments, I am left wondering whether that impression was incorrect. But I choose to believe that the United States Senate can still be the world’s greatest deliberative body and that young people can, in fact, have a say in our shared future. Senator Slotkin’s remarks should be an exception to how the Senate operates, not the rule. Thankfully, her threat could not have come at a more prescient time. The midterms are only two weeks away. Senator Slotkin’s words are not empty; they are a game plan for what Democrats will do if they retake power in Congress this November. Unfortunately, running that game plan will come at the expense of young men and women interested in serving their country. More still, in that very same discussion, Senator Slotkin left the door open to running for president in 2028. It is far from inconceivable that two years from now, we’ll be welcoming President-elect Slotkin into the Oval Office. That is why it is more important than ever that young conservatives speak out and show up. It doesn’t matter whether you have a Ph.D. from Harvard or dropped out of high school — your voice matters in this country. If you love our country and have the capacity to serve in government, I encourage you to do so. I recognize that that is not an easy ask. If Senator Slotkin is serious — and there is little reason to think she is not — serving your country will come at a great personal cost. Some very powerful people will seek to make you a pariah, as the host remarked to Senator Slotkin during her interview. And during the Biden administration, Democrats in the White House and Congress did so to many young conservatives. And one cannot forget Charlie Kirk’s assassination last September at the hands of a radical gunman. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But the hardest fights are also the most important ones to win. Should our government fall into the hands of those who seek power for revenge and target the weak, our fates will be at the will of tyrants. Preventing such a future requires the involvement of young people. John Adams once remarked to a crowd of young patriots in Philadelphia, "America and the world will look to our youth as one of our firmest bulwarks." 250 years after our nation’s founding, Adams’s words ring more true than ever before. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP So, do not cower in the face of Senator Slotkin’s threats. In fact, take her threats as a reason to serve our country. I sincerely believe that the fate of our Republic depends on it.

articles.title: Voters prepare to weigh-in on Trump's economy as costs continue to surge
articles.summary: Gas prices surged 9.1% in September as consumer prices rose 3.7% annually, putting Trump's promise to lower costs to the test before midterms.
articles.body: While Americans prepare to cast their ballots for who should control Congress and their local governments, the cost of filling a gas tank, paying rent and buying a home is becoming a defining test of the economy leading up to the 2026 midterms. The latest inflation report underscores the challenge facing President Donald Trump and Republicans as they campaign on the economy and the vow to improve conditions for American consumers. Trump returned to the White House promising to lower costs and is now campaigning for GOP candidates in key races — but the reality is something quite different. With Election Day two weeks away, rising prices are testing whether voters feel like Republicans have done enough to improve the economy and their financial well-being. AMERICAN-MADE GOODS ALSO GOT MORE EXPENSIVE UNDER TRUMP TARIFFS, NEW RESEARCH FINDS And that pressure showed up in the latest inflation report, which found consumer prices rose 3.7% over the past year and 0.6% in September alone. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks the prices households pay for a broad range of goods and services, from food and gasoline to housing and medical care. Gasoline was a major driver, with its index jumping 9.1% for the month. But the gas to fill up the tank is not the only fuel cost putting pressure on households. The diesel used to power trucks, farm equipment and freight trains is also surging, which has raised the cost of moving groceries, packages and building materials — another charge that has trickled down to how much Americans pay for those goods. Additionally, the Iran war has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, further tightening global fuel supplies, while disruptions to Russian energy infrastructure have added pressure. Utility costs are adding to the squeeze as colder weather approaches. Electricity prices were up 4.4% from a year earlier in September, while piped natural gas service rose 5%, according to the CPI. Those figures track prices, not what any one household paid, so a local customer’s bill can show how the increase is landing in real life. REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE. Housing costs also continued to climb. The shelter index, which tracks rents and a measure of what homeowners would pay to rent their homes, rose 3.2% over the past year. Grocery prices offered some relief, dipping 0.1% in September, though they remained 1.8% higher than a year earlier. Additionally, Trump's trade agenda is another part of the affordability debate. A New York Fed study found that tariffs in place through February added 2.9 percentage points to consumer-goods inflation. Tariffs are taxes on imported goods, and U.S. companies that pay them can pass some of the added cost along to shoppers. The study found that higher prices also reached some goods made in the United States, as domestic producers faced less competition from imports. The White House has argued that its trade policies will strengthen U.S. manufacturing and that foreign exporters bear the costs. Housing presents a different affordability challenge. The median price of an existing home reached $417,500 in September, up 1.3% from a year earlier, while the average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.4%. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The latest figures give voters a snapshot of what they are paying, but not a verdict on who is to blame. With Election Day approaching, Trump and Republican candidates will have to convince voters that their policies can make everyday costs more manageable.

articles.title: Trump puts fraudsters on notice with $25M whistleblower program offering cash for tips that deliver
articles.summary: President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance will unveil a $25 million fraud whistleblower program offering up to $30,000 for tips leading to convictions.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE - President Donald Trump is putting cash behind his crackdown on taxpayer fraud, preparing to offer Americans rewards for tips that help bring fraudsters to justice. Trump and Vice President JD Vance will unveil a $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP) during a Tuesday afternoon announcement with the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud in the Oval Office, a White House official told Fox News Digital. WHIP will offer eligible tipsters up to $30,000 if their information leads to a successful fraud conviction or a significant federal enforcement action, the official said. TRUMP'S WAR ON FRAUD EXPANDS AS TREASURY LAUNCHES NEW SITE WITH WHISTLEBLOWER INCENTIVES Trump also plans to present independent journalist Nick Shirley with a $10,000 check for his work exposing suspected fraud in Minnesota, according to the official. "Every day, President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud is zeroing in on the rampant abuse of taxpayer dollars and giving Americans the accountability they deserve. This administration has zero tolerance for individuals who steal from Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. EXCLUSIVE: NICK SHIRLEY FIRES BACK AT MINNESOTA CRITICS: 'NUMBERS DON'T LIE, AND CONVICTIONS DON'T LIE' The Justice Department will administer the new program, and Americans will be able to submit tips through fraud.gov, the official said. The initiative aims to encourage both independent journalists and everyday Americans to flag suspected fraud involving taxpayer money. Shirley drew national attention in December 2025 after publishing a video questioning whether several Somali-run Minnesota daycare centers were operating as legitimate businesses. His video showed apparently empty facilities and included people who said they had not seen children at the locations. AG BLANCHE UNVEILS FEDERAL CHARGES AGAINST 160 DEFENDANTS IN PANDEMIC RELIEF SWEEP The White House credited Shirley’s reporting with helping spur a surge of FBI and Department of Homeland Security resources into Minnesota, followed by investigations, arrests and new charges. One facility featured in Shirley’s video was Future Leaders Early Learning Center, whose former CEO, Fahima Egeh Mahamud, pleaded guilty in July to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States. HOUSE GOP BILL MOVES TO CLOSE WHISTLEBLOWER GAPS EXPOSED BY MINNESOTA MEDICAID FRAUD SCANDAL Prosecutors said Mahamud stole more than $4.6 million through false child care assistance claims and $850,000 through a federal child nutrition program connected to the Feeding Our Future scandal. Shirley previously pointed to Mahamud’s guilty plea as vindication of his reporting amid efforts to discredit his investigations. WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD "Well, numbers don't lie, and convictions don't lie either," he previously told Fox News Digital. The reward initiative adds a public tip incentive to the administration’s broader campaign against fraud in federal benefits programs. TRUMP SAYS ANTI-FRAUD EFFORTS ARE UNCOVERING BILLIONS IN WASTE, CLAIMS SAVINGS COULD BALANCE BUDGET Trump established the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud in March, with Vance serving as chairman. The executive order directed the group to coordinate efforts across federal agencies to uncover fraud, strengthen eligibility checks and prevent improper payments. Under the new program, submitting an allegation alone would not qualify someone for a reward. The tip must lead to a successful fraud conviction or a significant federal enforcement action, according to the White House official. articles.title: Trump’s approval ratings plummet: what that means for the US midterms
articles.summary: Sitting presidents usually see a dip in approval ratings before midterms, but Trump’s ratings are at a historic low.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s approval ratings have fallen to a record low, a sign that Americans angry about rising living costs amid the deeply unpopular US-Israel war on Iran could punish his party at the upcoming midterm elections.

Most Americans are unhappy with Trump’s performance, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Monday, with more people saying they plan to vote for Democrats on November 3.

Sitting US presidents have traditionally seen a dip in approval ratings around the midterms, and that has often coincided with their parties losing seats in Congress.

With Trump’s ratings lower than any of his predecessors, experts say Democrats could reach their goal of flipping both the US House of Representatives and the Senate in the congressional vote.

All 435 districts in the House and 33 of the 100 Senate seats are up for election.

Republicans currently hold a slim majority of 218-214 seats in the House, and are also leading in the Senate, with a 53-47 majority. However, Democrats are campaigning hard to seize majorities in both houses, a scenario that could prove a major headache for Trump.

Here’s what the latest polls might mean for these elections:

About 31 percent of Americans polled by Reuters/Ipsos said they were happy with Trump’s performance – the lowest-ever figure during Trump’s two terms as president. Two weeks earlier, the number stood at 32 percent.

When asked which party they would vote for if the midterms were held today, 47 percent chose Democrats, while 35 percent opted for Republicans. That represents a 12-point advantage for the Democrats, the widest ever in the current cycle, and is up from the seven-point lead two weeks ago.

The slide in support for Republicans came from the growing number of women choosing Democrats – about half of those polled. More voters – 40 percent – also said Democrats were better at managing the economy, compared with 33 percent who selected Republicans.

The polls, which canvassed 1,679 adults, are a generic ballot providing an overview of voter sentiment, but not a state-by-state breakdown, meaning the results could still be surprising.

The president and party in charge of the White House usually face some backlash in the midterms.

Supporters of the non-presidential party are often more motivated to vote in the midterms than their counterparts, according to the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics.

The think tank also found that in 12 of the past 20 midterm elections since 1946, the sitting president’s approval ratings worsened between July and November, the months just before the elections. Only in seven instances did approval ratings improve, while in one case, during the 2006 elections under President George W Bush, the president’s approval ratings stayed the same.

What has that pattern meant for midterm results?

With a dip in presidential ratings being the norm, a more favourable view of the sitting president still often correlates with the governing party losing fewer seats in the midterms, according to researchers.

When presidential approval ratings are much lower, the party in power often loses more seats.

In the 20 midterm elections held since 1946, the governing party lost seats in the House of Representatives in 18 instances, although a well-liked president often cushioned the effect, according to data from The American Presidency Project run by the University of California (UC), Santa Barbara.

For example, Americans’ favourable view of President George Bush – 75 percent in the 1990 midterms – saw Republicans lose only eight seats across the two houses.

But research aggregating the UC Santa Barbara data found that when presidents have approval ratings below 50 percent, their party was likely to have a bad election.

In 1994, for example, when President Bill Clinton’s first midterm approval rating stood at 46 percent, Democrats lost 52 seats in Congress.

But when Clinton’s approval rose to 66 percent by the next midterms in 1998, Democrats lost only five seats.

Researchers say Trump’s plummeting ratings amid the US-Israel war on Iran are highly likely to affect Republicans negatively.

With Trump’s generally low ratings – the lowest of any president in US history, according to UC Santa Barbara’s aggregate – researchers say the odds that Republicans will keep their thin majority in Congress are very small.

The question, however, remains just how badly the party could be hurt by Trump’s policies.

Republicans might have some hope yet. According to the Center for Politics, presidential approval in the past five midterms has generally been slightly higher in exit polls than in pre-election polling, because those later surveys include people who have actually voted.

That means the midterm results ultimately hinge on how well parties convince supporters to actually cast their ballots.

How many seats could the Democrats take?

According to NBC News, which conducts its own polling and provides state-by-state breakdowns, Senate Democrats are likely to win North Carolina and Maine from the Republicans. NBC also sees Alaska, Iowa and Texas as states that could go either way.

In the House of Representatives, NBC predicts “possible flips” from Republican to Democrat in 15 districts. It rates four districts currently held by Republicans and three held by Democrats as “toss-up”.

If the Democrats were to win all of those close contests without losing any of their current seats, they would gain a total of 22 seats in the House of Representatives and five in the Senate.

articles.title: Midwest pro-Trump state could hold key to Republicans' midterm hopes
articles.summary: Tom Emmer warns Iowa GOP supporters that turnout will decide whether House Republicans keep their majority as three districts face tough races.
articles.body: DES MOINES, Iowa — House Republicans are pinning hopes of keeping their majority on a state that President Donald Trump won by roughly 13 points in November 2024. And while Iowa has leaned red in recent years, Republicans are now finding themselves defending three of its four congressional districts as polls give Democrats more hope by the day that the key to a blue wave runs through the Midwest. But Republicans are dismissing public perception surveys as a political cudgel used by the media and the left to discourage GOP voters, while insisting the results will come down to one thing. "Nobody knows what's going to happen on November 3. But I'm here to tell you, if our people show up, we win. If our people don't show up … then we're going to be scratching and clawing to hang on to every inch that we've got," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., told a room of GOP supporters in Dubuque, Iowa, on Thursday. MEDIA NARRATIVE PREDICTING BLUE WAVE IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE NOT MESHING WITH LOCAL REPUBLICANS: 'FIRED UP' Fox News Digital joined Emmer and several other House Republicans on a two-district swing in Iowa late last week. The No. 3 House GOP leader spent his afternoon at an event for congressional candidate Joe Mitchell in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, followed by a fundraiser for Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa, in Des Moines in the evening. At both events, he argued that polling showing Democrats with a growing advantage was incorrect, but he and others are still warning that getting Republicans out to vote will be key to the party’s success. "Republicans do not like to participate in surveys," Emmer told people Thursday evening in Des Moines. "We are very suspicious of the people who are giving the information to and the databases they’re putting us in. By the way, there are Republicans who answer these surveys who may tell exactly the opposite of what they actually stand on, because again, we don’t trust them." CRITICAL HOUSE RACE THAT COULD DECIDE CONTROL OF CONGRESS HITS HOME STRETCH AS GOP REP WARNS WHAT'S AT STAKE Fox News Power Rankings show all but one of Iowa’s four congressional districts are in play. Nunn’s district and the one represented by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, both "lean Democrat." The seat Mitchell is vying to take over from retiring Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, is ranked a "toss-up." Republicans across the country are privately worrying that Trump’s low approval numbers coupled with some of his more unpopular policies could drag down the GOP. Add in the overall high cost of living and gas prices, some on the right are bracing for a 2018-style blue wave. TRUMP’S BEEF IMPORT SCHEME WREAKS HAVOC ON FED-UP RED STATE CATTLE RANCHERS Two of the policies that could sandbag Republican candidates in Iowa in particular are Trump’s tariffs and his decision to import foreign beef. The agriculture-heavy state has been hit particularly hard so far, with tariffs making farm equipment and other materials more expensive, while Trump's trade war with China has hit American farmers hard with Beijing's retaliation. Trump has sought to mitigate the impact of his steel tariffs in particular, announcing plans last month for a $15 billion steel plant in Lee County, Iowa. But both Nunn and Mitchell are confident in the races they are running. TRUMP-LINKED SUPER PAC PULLS FUNDING FROM 2 HOUSE REPUBLICANS AS GOP FIGHTS TO KEEP MAJORITY "We feel very confident about the race. And that's because we've talked to every voter we can, asked for their vote on November 3, and we've been traveling the district for the last 13 months — all 22 counties, rural and suburban and urban, telling people, this is an election of common sense versus crazy," Mitchell told Fox News Digital. "We have the hardest workers on the ballot." Nunn told attendees at his event, "Not only is Iowa at the front line of the entire country when it comes to making sure we've got three competitive House seats, Des Moines, Iowa, the third district, our proud district, is now one of the most competitive in the country." "So not only are we on the front line, we get to be at the tip of the spear," Nunn said, weeks after he led a bipartisan bill aimed at curbing Trump's imports of foreign beef. And despite the national-level outlook on Trump, turning out the president’s supporters could be the difference between narrowly keeping the GOP majority and losing control of the House. TRUMP SAYS POLLS 'DON'T ACCOUNT FOR ONE THING,' AS HE PLEDGES TO DEFEAT COMMUNISTS 'ONCE AND FOR ALL' Trump, for his part, is doing what he can to motivate the base. Nunn kicked off his Thursday evening event shortly after a phone call with Trump, during which the president said he "is committed to making sure we remain here in Iowa," the congressman said. Trump is also set to descend on the state later this week for a rally in Sioux City, though it’s taking place in the only safe district for Republicans in the state. "I'm always competing. I don't care if it's Iowa, I don't care if it's Pennsylvania, Ohio, Nevada, Texas, Florida, they're all important to this midterm," Emmer told Fox News Digital. "This midterm, to me, will come down to about 10 seats. Everybody talks about 20-plus. No. It's going to be a very narrow end, and for Republicans, Iowa is a great example. If the Republicans come out to vote, we're going to be just fine." If the fate of the House majority did come down to the results of just 10 seats, that would mean Iowa would be responsible for roughly one-third of that success. And while not all Republicans are as confident in the GOP’s chances in Iowa, they do agree that the final results will come down to turnout. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This goes one of two ways — and both aren’t great for Republicans. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Joe Mitchell, and Zach Nunn either win by the skin of their teeth or it’s complete and total obliteration on November 3," a GOP operative familiar with campaigns in Iowa told Fox News Digital. "There is no in-between. If Republican voters turn out to the polls, there’s hope. If not, it’s going to be bad."

articles.title: 5 hottest midterm battlegrounds two weeks out from Election Day
articles.summary: In today’s issue: Election Day is fast approaching with voters now able to cast early ballots in many states throughout the country. Polls are continuing to show Democrats poised for a strong performance two weeks from today, but how much they can gain is still up in the air. All eyes are on a handful…
articles.body:
Election Day is fast approaching with voters now able to cast early ballots in many states throughout the country.

Polls are continuing to show Democrats poised for a strong performance two weeks from today, but how much they can gain is still up in the air. All eyes are on a handful of key states that are most crucial to both parties’ success next month.

Here’s the five biggest battleground states to watch down the home stretch.

The battle for the Senate could very well come down to the Lone Star State, as state Rep. James Talarico (D) and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) are battling in a razor-tight contest.

Talarico has narrowly led in most polls against Paxton, but it’s usually been within the margin of error. He’s trying to defy recent political history to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas in nearly 40 years.

At the same time, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) is seeking a fourth term against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa . The race was originally not expected to be particularly competitive, but it’s shown signs of tightening in these final months.

Texas Republicans are also hoping to make gains in the House following their mid-decade redistricting move last year, but that may be easier said than done .

Of all the Senate seats that Democrats are defending this year, outgoing Sen. Gary Peters ’s (D-Mich.) open seat may be the most high-profile.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed , a former Wayne County health director, and Mike Rogers , a former GOP congressman, have rallied with national figures in what’s often been a nasty fight. Those tensions were on display at the candidates’ first debate earlier this month and may be again at their next meeting Wednesday.

El-Sayed has consistently held a lead in polling over Rogers in the final months, but by no more than a few points . That’s close enough that even a small polling error — let alone a big miss like in the Democratic primary — could shift the outcome considerably.

Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) is favored to win the state’s open governor’s race against Rep. John James (R-Mich.). The results in these marquee contests could also have implications for a few key House races downballot.

Iowa has shifted away from Democrats in the past few election cycles, but the party is hoping to make gains in several races that could shake up the state’s leadership in D.C. and Des Moines.

State Auditor Rob Sand (D) is favored by Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) to win the gubernatorial race as he faces Republican businessman Zach Lahn . Democrats haven’t won the Iowa governor’s mansion in 20 years.

The true toss-up race in the Hawkeye State is the Senate race between Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D). If Democrats can win the seat, they would be in strong position to take control of the Senate.

At the same time, three out of four of the state’s congressional districts appear to be seriously competitive. Republicans swept all four in 2024.

The Buckeye State is another state that’s shifted red in the Trump era yet has competitive Senate and gubernatorial races this year.

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown , perhaps Democrats’ top recruit of the cycle, is attempting a political comeback after a narrow loss two years ago. He’s a well-known brand in Ohio and is seeking to leverage that against Sen. Jon Husted (R), who was appointed to his seat just last year to fill the vacancy from Vice President Vance .

Whoever wins the race will only hold the seat for two years before they need to run again in 2028.

Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton are battling in a governor’s race that appears just as competitive as the Senate contest. Acton started out as the underdog but is now narrowly favored in a toss-up race.

The most high-profile race in Pennsylvania this year may also be among the least competitive.

Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) has dominated the GOP nominee, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity , in polling and fundraising and by most analyses is expected to easily cruise to reelection. The bigger question is the length of Shapiro’s coattails.

Democrats are eyeing four congressional districts to flip this year, two of which saw Democratic incumbents lose in 2024. The Republicans are Reps. Ryan MacKenzie , Rob Bresnahan , Scott Perry and Brian Fitzpatrick .

DDHQ rates Perry as the most likely of the four to lose, while Fitzpatrick, who has developed a reputation as a moderate with cross-party appeal, is in the strongest spot. If Fitzpatrick’s race can at least get close on election night, it would be a strong sign for Democrats.

SMART TAKE with NewsNation’s BLAKE BURMAN

President Trump spent Monday in Kansas trying to boost the senate campaign of Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). Overall, our partners at Decision Desk HQ give Democrats a 56 percent chance of winning the upper chamber. I asked former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) who he believes would best be suited to control the Senate going forward. He offered this warning to his former party should they retake control.

“What they better do—hit the ground running and get the cost of living down. Get the debt down, get the cost of living down, get people’s lives in a better position if you want to lead,” Manchin told me. “If you’re going for retaliation and retribution, you’re going down a primrose path you can’t return from.”

Prices aren’t likely to suddenly and drastically get cheaper when we wake up on Nov. 4, no matter who wins. You can apply Manchin’s advice to either party going forward.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6p/5c on NewsNation.

Voters in oil-rich Alberta overwhelmingly rejected a referendum that would have directed the province to take steps toward a vote on declaring independence from Canada. About three-quarters of the votes favored remaining in Canada , a win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he pushes for national unity amid a standoff with Trump.

The Supreme Court declined to hear appeals from three men accused of plotting the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks who were seeking to reinstate plea deals they reached that the Pentagon nullified. Under the deals, the men were to plead guilty and give detailed confessions about their roles in exchange for the death penalty being taken off the table.

The Department of Justice has charged more than two dozen noncitizens in California on allegations that they have illegally voted or registered to vote . It’s the latest move in the administration’s push to eliminate noncitizen voting, an issue that is exceedingly rare .

FARM AID : The president announced an $8 billion program to provide relief for high diesel costs to farmers during a rally for Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) on Monday night.

An Agriculture Department release states that farmers will be able to receive a one-time payment from the fund.

The current cost of a gallon of diesel stands at about $6.32, according to AAA .

“Roger Marshall is the leader who fought for that to happen. Roger got it to happen,” Trump said of the program.

The announcement came as Trump sought to boost Marshall in the final weeks of what has become an unexpectedly close Senate race. Polls have shown Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton essentially tied in recent weeks, suggesting Democrats may be primed for a surprise flip.

Republicans have spent big on defending Marshall, with the GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund investing millions of dollars in the race in the final month.

Kansas hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in more than 90 years. DDHQ rates the race as “lean” Republican.

RED FLAG: A new Hatch Act complaint was filed against three Trump administration officials — Federal Communication Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr , Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — for campaigning earlier this month with Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

The complaint, filed by Democracy Defenders Fund and Reporters Without Borders, alleges that after Trump introduced Burgum and Lutnick by their official titles, they did not “ correct the impression that each was speaking officially,” so they “appear to have used their official positions while engaged in political activity ,” which directly violates the Hatch Act.

Carr, meanwhile, noted that he was speaking in a personal capacity, according to the complaint, but “his short remarks were focused on past and pending work of the FCC.” After the rally, Carr addressed the upcoming FCC vote on an Alaskan broadband deal, writing on X, “I look forward to working with @SenDanSullivan to get the job done.”

“This is an absurd attempt by a leftist group, that is led by an Obama era political appointee, to push baseless claims,” an Interior Department spokesperson told The Hill when asked about the complaint, noting Burgum was speaking in his personal capacity.

FEMALE FOCUS: Trump signed an executive order to bolster federal research on women’s health, establishing the Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health and creating a new task force at the White House.

The president credited first lady Melania Trump with pushing for the initiative, and he said the White House Women’s Health Task Force will be led by his chief of staff, Susie Wiles , and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The first lady introduced the order from the White House Rose Garden yesterday, saying it “establishes a new standard for women’s health in America.” She said the first task force meeting would take place later in the day.

STRONGMEN SUMMIT : Trump said he is open to participating in a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping .

“I would do it,” Trump told reporters yesterday, after The Wall Street Journal reported Putin earlier this month proposed a trilateral meeting to discuss the war in Ukraine.

But Trump suggested the topic of such a meeting would be “not so much on Ukraine” but rather, “We would have it to talk about weapons and denuclearization,” among other things.

Trump has come under fire, even from members of his own party, for his decision to waive sanctions on Russia to buy diesel from the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky denounced the move by saying the U.S. “is on the wrong side of history.”

“Maybe it’s time for Zelensky to get someone else to negotiate,” Trump told reporters Monday, when asked about the Ukrainian leader’s remarks.

TEEING OFF : The Trump administration is embroiled in a tense legal fight over the president’s plan to shut down and renovate East Potomac Park to turn the sprawling piece of public land into a championship-style golf course.

Tensions reached a fever pitch last week after U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes , an appointee of former President Biden , scolded lawyers for the federal government over the removal of hundreds of trees from the park without providing the judge additional notice. Reyes also barred further tree-cutting work at East Potomac and is weighing a possible extension of the temporary restraining order.

But the Trump administration has taken aim at the judge, who is presiding over the case brought by a preservationist group and individual golfers, accusing her of bias and requesting she recuse herself from the case — a request she refused in a 13-page opinion released late Sunday.

“By any objective measure, the Government fails to meet the standard for recusal,” Reyes wrote in the opinion denying the request.

The president called Reyes “a crazed lunatic” and “insane” on social media. Minutes before a hearing began yesterday, Trump posted on Truth Social that the administration does not need approval from the court to move ahead with the controversial redevelopment, which includes a total revamp of East Potomac Golf Links and the erasure of miles of walking and biking trails on the island.

During the hearing, questions were raised surrounding what Interior Department officials knew about the renovation plans. Trump has said plans for renovation were already in place and set to begin on Nov. 15, when the existing public golf courses there would be closed.

Jessica Bowron , the acting director of the National Park Service, testified earlier Monday that she was not aware of plans to close the course in mid-November.

“I don’t know what to do when I keep getting different stories from the government,” Reyes said during the hearing.

SEIZING THE MOVEMENT : Republicans are seizing on protests that have rocked France to point the finger at liberals and an immigration system they say has gotten out of hand.

French President Emmanuel Macron urged the public for calm as protests descended into rioting and looting over the weekend, vowing that “those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.” He blamed the “unrestrained violence” on “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups.”

The protests initially began at a high school in a Paris suburb, focused on teacher shortages and deteriorating building conditions. But it’s spread across the country and resulted in fringe riots that have led to clashes between police and French protesters.

Trump and Vance have both alleged mass immigration into France is to blame for the riots.

“The migrants have taken over France,” Trump wrote Monday morning on Truth Social. “They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!”

Vance tied the situation to what he said would happen if Democrats win back power in the midterms.

“I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn,” he said over the weekend. “And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.”

The Hill’s Helen Huiskes reports how the protests are becoming the latest pitch for embattled Republicans as they make a final effort to tie Democrats to socialism and out-of-control immigration before the midterms. Her latest edition of the newsletter The Movement will be out later this morning with the deep dive.

And finally … Next year will mark the end of an era as longtime CNN chief international anchor Christiane Amanpour announced Monday that she will leave the network in June.

Amanpour has worked at CNN for 43 years, first joining the network’s foreign desk in 1983. She served as its chief international correspondent for nearly 20 years and has hosted “Amanpour” on CNN International since 2009.

Amanpour said she made the decision after “many months of thought” and is looking forward to “interesting new projects down the line.” CNN noted that she had scaled back her hosting to a few days a week in January 2025 and will shift to once per week in January 2027 until the program ends in May.

Amanpour thanked the network and the teams she worked with covering a wide range of global conflicts, including the Bosnian War, Gulf War, Rwandan genocide and Afghanistan War.

articles.title: Inside the monthslong federal investigation of Rep. Ilhan Omar
articles.summary: Scott Johnson, a retired Minnesota attorney and co-founder of Powerline Blog, first began looking into Omar in 2016.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The creator of a conservative blog who was among the first to raise questions surrounding Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar says federal agents interviewed him in January 2026, suggesting authorities were building a case before the congresswoman’s home was raided in October.

Scott Johnson, a retired Minnesota attorney and co-founder of Powerline Blog, first began looking into Omar in 2016, when she first ran for local office.

Johnson tells NewsNation he received an unexpected call earlier this year to meet with two federal agents in Minnesota, eight months before the October raid on Omar’s Washington, D.C. home.

“In January of this year, I was contacted by two ICE agents who asked me to meet with them, and this was in the middle of Operation Metro Surge,” Johnson said.

“They asked me questions that related to issues of (Omar’s) immigration and naturalization and also questions related to her father, which would bear on the same issue,” he said. “So I inferred at the end of that hour, and from other help that they asked me for, that they were looking at a possible civil proceeding that might lead to her denaturalization.”

Johnson said agents had a “detailed knowledge” of her case when he met with them in January.

“(The investigation has) obviously carried on since then. They’ve obviously filled out the case, and I would say there must be many agents involved, and they’ve gone down several different trails,” he said.

Johnson said they asked him for documents and files related to Omar and came back to meet with him a second time to discuss some of his early sources in Minnesota’s Somali community.

The developments come amid reporting from NewsNation’s Leland Vittert that federal agents collected garbage in hopes of obtaining DNA from Omar and her family before the raid at the Minnesota Democrat’s home in Washington, D.C.

Multiple sources familiar with the probe tell NewsNation potential DNA evidence is critical to the investigation into Omar. They say the case is broader than the public may assume based on longstanding accusations surrounding her immigration history and marital status.

The investigation encompasses the congresswoman’s family members, with evidence expected to be presented to a grand jury, sources said. Relatives of the lawmaker have been named in some of the subpoenas issued by federal prosecutors, NewsNation has reported.

The 44-year-old Omar, who seeks a fifth term in Congress, was born in Somalia in 1982 , came to the U.S. around the age of 12 and about five years later became a U.S. citizen through her father.

Omar was investigated by the Department of Justice under President Biden, a Democrat, before the case was closed. Parts of that investigation were reopened and expanded under the administration of President Trump, a Republican.

Omar, a frequent political foil for Trump, says the DOJ has been weaponized against her.

She has not been seen publicly since the raid on her home but called it an “outrageous abuse of power ” in a social media post.

articles.body: Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico skipped a Monday night rally headlined by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., in El Paso, instead holding campaign events hundreds of miles away in North Texas as his closely watched race against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton enters its final weeks. Sanders appeared at the Abraham Chavez Theatre alongside former Rep. Beto O'Rourke and Democratic Reps. Greg Casar and Veronica Escobar as early voting began ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. JAMES TALARICO RESURFACES AFTER EXTENDED ABSENCE AS HIS CAMPAIGN PUSHES BACK Fox News Digital reached out to Talarico's campaign for comment on why the candidate held a separate event instead of campaigning with the other Democrats, who used the El Paso event to promote his Senate bid and criticize Republican campaign spending. "They have spent, so far, $368 million just against one man, the next senator from the state of Texas, James Talarico. That's how desperate, how scared and how panicked they are right now," O'Rourke told supporters. DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS Casar also expressed support for Talarico, telling the crowd that electing him would help advance Democrats' legislative priorities. Sanders, who did not mention Talarico by name during his remarks, instead directed his criticism toward wealthy political donors and their influence on American elections. "What you are seeing in this campaign, what you are seeing right here in Texas, all over America, is multibillionaires are pouring hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars," Sanders said. The Vermont Independent urged supporters to vote early, casting the midterms as a battle over the political influence of wealthy Americans. At his separate Fort Worth rally, Talarico delivered a similar message about money in politics, targeting Paxton and billionaire Elon Musk over the influence of wealthy donors in the Texas Senate race. TALARICO SAYS THE DIVIDE IS 'TOP VS. BOTTOM' — THEN HEADS TO ONE OF AMERICA'S RICHEST DONOR ENCLAVES "We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis," Talarico told supporters. He also sought to frame his candidacy as an appeal beyond traditional party divisions. "This election shouldn't be about the Democratic Party or the Republican Party. It's bigger than that," he said. articles.title: How did being a good teammate become so controversial?
articles.summary: Athletes cannot be celebrated for speaking out when their views fit comfortably within worldviews compatible with the establishment, but then become professionally expendable when they say something that makes others uncomfortable.
articles.body:
How did Sophie Cunningham simply living her life and being a good teammate turn into a reason for somebody to say she should lose her job? That is really what we are talking about here. Candace Buckner of The Athletic says the Indiana Fever should move on from Cunningham because she has become “too combustible” and her opinions are “too turbulent” to be paired with Caitlin Clark.

And once again, Cunningham is back in the headlines not because of something she did, but because of what someone else is saying about her. The reaction to Buckner’s column then became its own story .

But what does “too combustible” really mean? It is hard to square with what Cunningham has actually done. She stood up for a teammate, became popular because fans appreciated it, and later answered questions about what she believes. Other people took those answers and turned them into weapons in a culture war basketball is now deeply embroiled in.

Go back to where this started. Cunningham did not become famous because she went looking for a political fight. She became famous after Caitlin Clark was poked in the eye and knocked to the floor during a physical game against Connecticut, and Cunningham made it clear she had her teammate’s back. Fans noticed, and her Instagram following jumped by nearly 300,000, her TikTok following climbed from about 300,000 to more than 1.2 million. Her Fever jersey also sold out.

That is the irony here. Buckner says Indiana needs to get back to basketball, but Cunningham’s rise into the spotlight started with basketball. She was being a good teammate on the court.

Then came a wide-ranging ESPN profile . Cunningham discussed the political assumptions people make about her and gave her view on protecting girls’ and women’s sports from male competition and intrusion into female spaces. She also said she wanted to “extend love” and rejected the idea that she hated transgender people.

That helped light the cultural fuse. Protests and counterprotests began surrounding Fever games , while the Trump White House publicly praised Cunningham’s position .

Before long, Cunningham stopped being just a basketball player in the public imagination. Some critics used her as a sword in the culture war, casting her as a new face of transphobia in women’s sports . Others used her as a shield for their worldview, holding her up as someone willing to defend girls’ and women’s sports. Both sides projected something onto her, and now Buckner looks at all of that reaction and treats Cunningham herself as the problem.

That is where I lose the argument. Cunningham did not organize the protests, summon the politicians or create the national debate over women’s sports. She answered questions and people reacted. Then they took all that noise and put it back on her. It’s a form of circular reasoning: External actors created the controversy around Cunningham, then they blamed Cunningham for being controversial.

If she is hurting the Indiana Fever, show me the damage. Buckner does not point to teammates rejecting Cunningham, coaches saying she is unmanageable or Clark saying she wants her gone. Instead, the case is built around the reaction Cunningham generates outside the locker room.

There is also a double standard here that some people in sports media need to examine. For years we have heard that athletes should use their platforms, speak their truth and refuse to “stick to sports.” I am fine with that. Megan Rapinoe can give her opinion, and I may disagree with her or debate her all day long, but I would never argue that she should lose her livelihood simply because I do not like what she believes.

But that principle has to go both ways in a society that says it values free speech and the exchange of ideas. Athletes cannot be celebrated for speaking out when their views fit comfortably within worldviews compatible with the establishment, but then become professionally expendable when they say something that makes others uncomfortable.

That is why Buckner’s argument deserves more scrutiny. She has previously argued that “sticking to sports never made sense” and that athletes inevitably exist inside the larger culture. But when Cunningham’s place in that culture becomes uncomfortable, the answer is effectively to remove the player from the equation.

If Cunningham’s baggage outweighs her value, make that case. Teams make those decisions every day, but public reaction alone should not be proof that a player has become a problem.

Maybe the bigger story is not Cunningham at all — maybe it is us. Cunningham is playing basketball, supporting teammates and enjoying the fans who embraced her, while the rest of us fight over what she supposedly represents.

When a basketball player cannot be a good teammate, answer a question honestly and go about her life without everyone reaching for the cultural knives, that says more about our culture than it does about her. Sophie Cunningham did not create all this noise. We did, and maybe we should stop blaming her for it.

Rich Herrera is host of “Richmond’s Morning News” on NewsRadio WRVA, a cable news contributor and a veteran of national sports radio and professional sports broadcasting.

articles.title: 33 percent say second attempt should follow failed execution: Survey
articles.summary: A third of Americans think that the government should try a second time to put 50-year-old Christa Pike to death after she survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection last month. A four-day Reuters/Ipsos poll found 33 percent American adults said a second attempt should be made to execute inmates who survive the…
articles.body:
A third of Americans think that the government should try a second time to put 50-year-old Christa Pike to death after she survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection last month.

A four-day Reuters/Ipsos poll found 33 percent American adults said a second attempt should be made to execute inmates who survive the first time, while 39 percent supported life in prison instead.

On Sept. 30, Pike received two doses of the state’s lethal injection drug pentobarbital and survived. She was taken to a Nashville area hospital in an ambulance, where she received medical care and regained consciousness five days after. She was later discharged from the hospital and is back at the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years.

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.

The latest poll showed 52 percent Republicans, compared to 24 percent Democrats, support a second execution attempt. About 55 percent of the Americans who responded to the poll supported the death penalty for people convicted ​of the most serious crimes, down from 63 percent from a 2017 poll, according to Reuters.

About 31 percent respondents opposed the death penalty, while 13 percent either skipped the question or said were not sure. A majority of Republicans, 80 percent, supported the death penalty in the latest poll, as opposed to 39 percent Democrats.

The nationwide poll was conducted online, gathering responses from 1,679 U.S. adults between Oct. 16-19. It had a margin of error of ​2 percentage points.

articles.body:
It’s Tuesday. We’re only two weeks out from November’s midterms.

Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com .

President Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday.

The talks are happening in Oslo, Norway, alongside leaders of Norway and Finland, according to the Norwegian government. Kushner will attend virtually.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a statement that Ukraine requested the U.S. representatives attend the meetings.

“Diplomatic efforts have previously taken place in several countries, and Norway and Finland are pleased to be able to continue this work. The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path,” he added.

Trump is getting mad : The president on Monday told reporters, “All I want for Russia and Ukraine is for them to stop the stupid war.”

“Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” he added. “If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago, and he’d have a million people living from his side.”

The president also said he would be willing to participate in a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to address how to stop the Russia-Ukraine war.

Putin proposed the summit during a call with Trump earlier this month, per a Wall Street Journal report that cited a Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter.

That phone conversation resulted in Trump’s announcement that he would waive sanctions on Russia to allow for more diesel sales in an effort to lower prices.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Monday he believes there’s been “talks of a meeting,” when asked about the report.

“I think the president is open to anything that he can do to help bring the war to an end if it’s possible,” Rubio added.

Starshield squabble still going strong: Last week, Elon Musk’s Starlink took the spotlight after Ukraine’s military faced restricted access to Starshield, the military version of the satellite-based system.

Starlink services were cut off for objects that traveled more than 100 mph, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill.

For days, senators and representatives have expressed concerns over Ukraine’s sudden loss of access to intelligence sharing and the high-speed Starlink data.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, as well as Republican Sens. Thom Tillis (N.C.), Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and John Cornyn (Texas) signed a letter to Platte Moring , the Pentagon’s inspector general, urging an investigation into the incident.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) on Monday said Zelensky told senators Ukraine still does not have full access to Starshield. Tillis and Blumenthal hosted a call with the Ukrainian president and other “bipartisan colleagues.”

“President Zelenskyy is ready for a mutual ceasefire on energy facilities & resources, & civilians, if only Putin will agree. Vicious, bloodthirsty slaughter by Russia’s missiles & drones is intensifying,” Blumenthal said on social media.

“Bipartisan, bicameral support for Ukraine was clear & unequivocal, which we’ll be expressing in upcoming action,” he added.

And GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.) on Monday said he’d speak with Zelensky, too. He vowed to hold any U.S. official who limited the application “ fully accountable .”

Vice President Vance said that if he ran for president in 2028, he thinks Trump would endorse him .

“I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race,” Vance said in an interview with 2WAY’s Mark Halperin on Monday.

“And because the president’s endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, ‘You know what? We need to let, like, this race play out and not preemptively prejudge the results.’”

But the vice president also avoided endorsing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of the country’s elections next week. “I’m not anti-endorsing him. I’m not pro-endorsing him,” he said.

He added that he was “not getting involved” and focusing on American politics. “I endorse American candidates,” he added.

During his Monday night rally in Wichita, Kan., President Trump announced an $8 billion program that will provide temporary relief to farms amid rising fuel and energy prices because of the Iran war.

As of Tuesday morning, the average price for a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. sits at $4.27, while diesel is $6.31 per gallon, according to AAA .

Farming for answers: Trump introduced the Harvest Fuel Relief program in a state that is reeling from the effects of the conflict in the Middle East.

This has fueled a tight Senate battle for GOP Sen. Roger Marshall , who has seen his polling lead dwindle to his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton .

A similar situation can be found in Iowa, where the Senate battle between Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and Democratic challenger Josh Turek is locked in a toss-up.

Hinson is among a group of GOP lawmakers that has bashed the U.S.’s diesel deal with Russia.

Sens. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.) are also among those who have criticized Trump’s moves.

Parts of the program: According to the Department of Agriculture, the $8 billion will be available as a one-time release for farmers.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said the program will provide “critical support to farmers facing rising costs and market disruptions.”

The president’s midterm campaign tour continues Tuesday night with a trip to Greenville, N.C., to campaign for GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley , who is facing off against former Gov. Roy Cooper (D).

According to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, Cooper, has a lengthy lead over Whatley, with an 84 percent chance to capture the Senate seat.

House up for grabs: Trump’s rally in the Tar Heel State will also focus on some tight House battles.

Greenville borders North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, which is listed by DDHQ as a toss-up between Democratic Rep. Don Davis and Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout .

The 3rd Congressional District, where Greenville sits, leans GOP, and incumbent Rep. Gregory Murphy (R) has a 78 percent chance to beat Democrat Raymond Smith , according to DDHQ.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers broke an American citizen’s arm over the weekend.

Garcia said in a Sunday post to the social platform X that “ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen.”

“I’m proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE. Donald Trump and his inhumane and illegal deportation machine must be stopped,” Garcia continued.

ICE in October: Earlier this month, Texas prosecutors said they were weighing criminal charges after allegations that an ICE officer intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston.

An ICE spokesperson told The Hill following the incident that, “As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

Meanwhile, surveillance video showed two men running when an SUV veered into and hit Parra-Hernandez.

In a report that came out over the weekend, an immigration advocacy group stated that the immigrant whom federal agents were pursuing when the incident occurred has apparently been dead for almost a decade.

In a separate incident in New York City on Oct. 8, a man was injured when an ICE officer shot him. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said the man had a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and multiple arrests for assault, robbery and drug possession.

Not going anywhere: After a man was shot by ICE in Austin, Texas last month, White House border czar Tom Homan emphasized that people can “hate us all you want,” but, “We’re not going anywhere.”

The FBI reportedly investigated whether former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.) were involved in a bribery scheme with Hawaiian naval defense contractor Navatek acquiring federal contracts in their home state, according to a ProPublica report.

A new video promoting Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R) tapped into Democratic challenger Amy Acton’s mom, who calls her daughter a “liar” in the video. Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns , called the video a “despicable low” for Ramaswamy.

articles.title: Trump, take this Russia deal: Ukraine stops hitting energy, expand Starshield!
articles.summary: The end to the war will be on Russia’s terms, and Ukraine’s terms, and our terms — but until Russia is ready to play ball, there’s no reason to let up.
articles.body:
The Ukraine War is again an all-consuming issue in American media, as President Trump continues to express frustration with Volodmyr Zelensky and Ukraine’s decision to continue destroying Russian energy production . Zelensky, however, understandably thinks this is necessary in order to beat Russia in this war, even though it damages the global economy and is indirectly harming Trump’s reelection prospects.

So here’s a plan: Ukraine should agree to stop hitting the energy infrastructure, and in exchange we will extend the use of SpaceX system Starshield from Ukrainian strikes within Ukraine itself to Russian territory.

The good news is Zelensky is already on board with this plan — here was Sen. Kevin Cramer, a Republican from North Dakota, telling “Face the Nation” all about it.

To that I say, let’s make a deal! We can leave Russian energy production, which the rest of the world counts on, intact. And instead, we can equip Ukraine with the ability to bring the fight to the enemy: to Russia.

Trump should like this plan, because his concern is that energy prices are hurting Republicans’ midterm chances by causing blowback against this war. The person who won’t like the plan is Vladirmir Putin, because he wants to keep wielding the threat of higher gas prices as a means of deterring Europe from fully backing the Ukrainian cause.

But from the U.S. perspective it’s a win-win. We don’t want to ease the pressure on Russia. We know Putin is feeling the pain, because now he wants to meet with Trump and Xi Jinping to discuss the end of the war. Such a negotiation, however, should be between Trump and Zelensky and Putin — let’s leave China out of it. In fact, his mere desire to bring in Xi for backup should be telling us everything we really need to know about who Putin is really beholden to. That would be our main rival: China.

So let’s give Ukraine the power to keep taking the fight to Russia, and to concentrate on Russian military targets, so that once the war is over Europe is free to buy Russian energy and we can all benefit from a shared prosperity. But that’s not happening until the war ends. The end will be on Russia’s terms, and Ukraine’s terms, and our terms — but until Russia is ready to play ball, there’s no reason to let up.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.
